papers.title: Effect of Rainfall Infiltration on the Hydromechanical Behavior of Slopes under Unsaturated Conditions
papers.summary: Nowadays, slopes forming transportation infrastructure are highly sensitive to hydraulic conditions such as rainfall, triggering negative impacts on ecosystems and road infrastructure. In this regard, this research analyzes the hydromechanical influence of a frequent rainfall intensity in northern Peru of 10 mm/h on the stability of slopes (T1, T2, and T3) under unsaturated conditions. For this purpose, simulations were performed using Plaxis 2D software, considering three slope geometries based on regulatory criteria for clayey gravel soils with fines content and groundwater table conditions. The input parameters for the soil were based on the Hardening Soil model, while the Van Genuchten model was used for flow analysis. The obtained results indicate that, within the analyzed section measured from the upper surface downward, maximum saturation reached a depth equivalent to 33% of the slope height for model T1, 11.8% for model T2, and 6.4% for model T3. In addition, the effective surface suction produced reductions lower than 3 kN/m² after 24 hours of continuous rainfall. Finally, the factor of safety was affected under the same scenario, decreasing by up to 59.11% for model T1, 49.2% for model T2, and 42.80% for model T3. It should be noted that the most significant transition toward instability occurred after 10 hours.

papers.title: Analysis of Landslide Susceptibility Toward the Presence of Accommodation Areas (Glamping and Villas) in Kejajar District, Wonosobo Regency, 2025
papers.summary: This study aims to analyze and map the level of landslide susceptibility in accommodation areas in Kejajar District, Wonosobo Regency, using a Geographic Information System (GIS) approach. Scoring, weighting, and overlay methods were applied to integrate rainfall, slope gradient, soil type, geology, and land-use parameters. The results indicate that Kejajar District is divided into three landslide susceptibility classes: high susceptibility covering 4,936 ha (76%), moderate susceptibility covering 1,515 ha (23%), and low susceptibility covering 37 ha (<1%). Spatial analysis of accommodation areas indicates that most villas and glamping facilities are located in moderate-to-high susceptibility zones, particularly in areas with steep slopes, high rainfall, and easily weathered soil materials. These findings emphasize the importance of using landslide susceptibility maps as a basis for spatial planning and disaster mitigation guidance in the development of highland tourism areas.

papers.title: The Effect of Collaborative Leadership and Early Warning System on Community Preparedness Response through Community Participation in Madiun Regency
papers.summary: Disaster risks in Madiun Regency, particularly floods, landslides, and tornadoes, underscore the need for preparedness strategies that integrate early warning systems, stakeholder coordination, and community involvement. This study examined the effects of collaborative leadership and early warning systems on community preparedness response, including indirect effects through community participation. A quantitative explanatory design involved 400 respondents from purposively selected areas. Data were collected using a five-point Likert-scale questionnaire and analyzed through partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) using SmartPLS 4. The structural model identified significant paths from collaborative leadership and early warning systems to both preparedness response and community participation. Community participation was positively and significantly associated with preparedness response and partially mediated the relationship between each predictor and preparedness response. These findings identify community participation as an intermediary linking collaborative leadership and early warning systems to preparedness. The study concludes that disaster preparedness efforts should integrate collaborative governance, warning systems, and community participation. The findings provide evidence to inform the strengthening of participatory disaster management policies in Madiun Regency.

Problems, causes and impacts of landslides along the Beni–Jomsom–Korala Road in the Kaligandaki Corridor, Nepal
papers.source: Universal Technical Journal of Lumbini International Academy of Science and Technology
papers.summary: The Beni–Jomsom–Korala road, part of the Kaligandaki Corridor linking Myagdi and Mustang districts with the northern border of Nepal, is repeatedly blocked by landslides, particularly during the monsoon. This study assessed the major landslide problems along the road, their causes and effects, and the mitigation measures preferred by stakeholders. A mixed-methods design was used, combining field observation of four active landslides (Baisari, Sirubari, Guithe Bhir and Suke Bagar), engineering geological maps of the Khamvitta and Tatopani slides, focus group discussions, in-depth interviews and a five-point Likert questionnaire answered by 120 engineers, contractors, officials and local stakeholders. Items were ranked with the Relative Importance Index (RII); internal consistency was checked with Cronbach’s alpha (0.767–0.921 across the four scales) and relations between constructs with Pearson correlation. River cutting and toe erosion by the Kaligandaki River (RII = 0.80) and cutting of the hillside to carve the road (0.78) were the most important of 19 problems, followed by inadequate drainage, poor lithology and weak geology (0.76 each). The leading causes were steep and unstable slopes (0.82), removal of the slope toe by road widening (0.82), communities living on unstable slopes (0.82), insufficient government funding (0.82) and fractured, weathered rock (0.80). The most important effects were water accumulation on the road causing erosion (0.84), increased casualties when rescue is delayed (0.83), delayed mitigation projects (0.83) and disruption of trade and tourism (0.82). Ratings of causes and effects were very strongly correlated (r = 0.863, p < 0.001). Field evidence confirmed fractured rock, shallow groundwater, river undercutting and blasting damage as the dominant mechanisms. Respondents ranked slope stabilization with retaining and breast walls (0.78), rock anchoring and netting, and roadside bioengineering (0.76 each) as the most important measures.

papers.title: Assessment of Flood Impacts, Losses and Adaptation Practices in Bhajani Municipality, Kailali District, Nepal

papers.summary: Floods are the most frequent and damaging hydro-meteorological hazard in the Terai region of Nepal, yet municipal-scale evidence that links hazard mapping, community perception, historical losses and local adaptation remains scarce. This study assesses flood impacts, losses, and adaptation practices in Bhajani Municipality, Kailali District, Sudurpashchim Province, a low-lying municipality with nine wards (176.25 km²) and crossed by the Mohana, Kandra, Kanda (Kadha), and Patharaiya rivers. A mixed-methods design combined a questionnaire survey of 156 respondents (Slovin’s formula, e = 8%), focus group discussions, in-depth interviews, field observation and desk review of the Local Disaster and Climate Resilience Plan (LDCRP). The Relative Importance Index (RII) was used to rank 16 flood-related problems, their causes and effects, and 12 adaptation measures rated on a five-point Likert scale; 64 Chi-square tests of independence examined whether perceptions differ by gender, age, occupation and education, and a GIS-based Weighted Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (WMCDA) using distance from rivers (30%), Topographic Wetness Index (25%), slope (25%) and Height Above Nearest Drainage (20%) produced a flood hazard map. Wards 3, 5, 7 and 8 were classified as very high flood-risk areas, wards 6 and 9 as high, wards 1 and 2 as moderate and ward 4 as low–moderate; 85 settlements and hamlets are potentially exposed. papers.title: Feature-engineered physics-conditioned DNN with validation-selected ridge residual correction for pore water pressure prediction in clays
papers.summary: Introduction Accurately predicting pore water pressure is important for evaluating effective stress, deformation, and stability in clayey soils. Methods This study develops an interpretable feature-engineered physics-conditioned DNN with validation-selected ridge residual correction using 42 complete curves from kaolin clay and Mercia Mudstone clay. Complete curves were divided into training, validation, and testing subsets. Three configurations were compared: a Physics-Conditioned DNN (PC-DNN), a feature-engineered PC-DNN (FE-PC-DNN), and the FE-PC-DNN with a candidate residual stage. Physical knowledge was used to select variables, construct hydro-mechanical interaction features, define a reference response, and bound the correction; governing equations were not enforced in the loss function. Results Validation assigned zero weight to the neural residual candidate and full weight to ridge regression. Accordingly, the reported residual correction was ridge-based, clipped to ±0.419394 kPa, and combined with a validation-bias offset of −0.099064 kPa. The ridge-corrected FE-PC-DNN achieved a test MSE of 1.58 kPa 2 , RMSE of 1.26 kPa, MAE of 0.82 kPa, and sMAPE of 8.75%. Global SHAP analysis identified soil type, axial strain, and confining pressure as the main features. A unified kernel-weighted B-spline equation, calibrated on 36 development curves and evaluated once on six locked test curves, achieved R 2 = 0.982, RMSE = 0.894 kPa, MAE = 0.716 kPa, and sMAPE = 6.03%. Discussion These results demonstrate strong internal performance within the tested two-soil domain; external validation is still required before field use.

papers.title: A Comprehensive County-Scale Dataset for Geohazard Risk Assessment of House Construction via Cutting Slope (HCCS)
papers.summary: House construction via cutting slope (HCCS) is an increasingly important driver of geohazards in the granite weathering regions of southeastern China. In these areas, frequent intense rainfall and the rapid growth of self-built rural housing together contribute to recurring landslides at HCCS sites. However, relevant geo-environmental data are often dispersed across survey reports in non-standardized formats, hindering their integration and reuse in fine-scale spatial analyses. We describe a county-wide geospatial dataset for Yanling County, Hunan Province, China, that links slope units, geohazard inventories, and HCCS sites within a unified spatial framework. The dataset includes 3478 slope units, 213 documented geohazard sites (landslides, debris flows, collapses, and ground subsidence), and 12,420 HCCS sites, as well as supporting layers including a digital elevation model, geological structures, river networks, and administrative boundaries. The data were generated from a 1:10,000 geohazard survey using a standardized workflow covering field investigation, database development, and multi-level review, and were further harmonized through unified coordinate and attribute systems. This dataset provides a rare fine-scale representation of the spatial coupling between anthropogenic slope modification for housing and rainfall-induced landslides at the individual-building scale. It offers a reusable data foundation for landslide susceptibility mapping, risk evaluation of HCCS development, and studies of coupled hazard processes in comparable granite mountainous environments.

papers.title: Comparative Machine Learning Approaches to Landslide Susceptibility in Southeastern Türkiye
papers.summary: Landslides are among the most destructive natural hazards in mountainous regions, causing severe economic losses and infrastructure damage. Reliable susceptibility mapping is essential for hazard mitigation and sustainable land-use planning, particularly in tectonically active areas such as southeastern Türkiye. This study aims to compare the predictive performance and spatial consistency of six widely used machine learning algorithms—Support Vector Machine (SVM), Logistic Regression (LR), Random Forest (RF), Artificial Neural Network (ANN), Naïve Bayes (NB), and Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt)—together with an Ensemble model, under identical geomorphological and environmental conditions. A GIS-based framework was applied using eleven conditioning factors derived from topographic, geological, hydrological, and land-cover datasets. A landslide inventory verified by field observations was used for model training and validation. Model performance was assessed using Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) analysis and the Area Under the Curve (AUC). All models achieved high predictive accuracy (AUC = 0.877–0.959). The NB model performed best (AUC = 0.959), while the Ensemble model produced the most spatially consistent susceptibility patterns. High- and very high-susceptibility zones were consistently associated with steep slopes and weak lithological units. Comparative machine learning approaches provide reliable and transferable tools for regional landslide susceptibility assessment. The results highlight the importance of algorithm selection and ensemble strategies in susceptibility mapping.

papers.title: Investigation on an Improved SegFormer with Multi-Module Fusion for Landslide Recognition in Remote Sensing Images
papers.summary: Landslides pose severe threats to life and property, necessitating rapid and accurate identification for effective hazard assessment and emergency response. This study proposes an improved SegFormer model for precise landslide extraction from high-resolution remote sensing imagery. To address the limitations of existing segmentation methods in handling complex backgrounds and irregular boundaries, the proposed framework integrates several structural enhancements. These include a squeeze-and-excitation module to suppress background noise, an auxiliary edge-fusion branch to capture explicit boundary details, and an adaptive feature gating mechanism to refine feature representation. The model is trained using focal loss to mitigate class imbalance and employs a three-stage recognition process, culminating in post-processing with dense conditional random fields for boundary refinement. Herein, the experimental results on a dataset of 100 high-resolution satellite images demonstrate that this approach outperforms the classical U-Net architecture and traditional thresholding techniques. The model achieved an accuracy of 0.976, a precision of 0.918, a recall of 0.947, and an F1-score of 0.932. These findings confirm that the proposed method offers exceptional accuracy and robustness, providing an effective automated tool for large-scale landslide detection in complex terrain.

Integrated multi-criteria decision analysis and bivariate statistical modeling for landslide susceptibility zonation in the northwestern Ethiopian highlands
papers.summary: Landslides represent a critical geo-environmental hazard in the Ethiopian highlands, specifically within the Telemt, Janamora, and Beyeda districts, where they frequently result in fatalities and the destruction of vital infrastructure and agricultural land. This study integrated Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and remote sensing data to perform landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM) using two distinct modeling approaches: the Frequency Ratio (FR) and the Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP). A total of 140 data points (98 for training (70%) and 42 for testing (30%)) were considered for modeling and validation. Eleven geo-environmental conditioning factors: Slope, rainfall, lithology, density of lineaments, curvature, aspect, normalized difference vegetation index, land use/land cover, distance to drainage, drainage density, and soil were analyzed to evaluate their influence on landslide occurrence. According to the AHP model, 13.69% and 26.91% of the study area were classified as very high and high susceptibility zones, respectively. In comparison, the FR model identified 12.09% as very high and 23.78% as high susceptibility zones. Both models underscored that steep slopes, porphyritic basalt unit, high lineament density, proximity to drainage systems, and concave terrain curvature are the primary drivers of slope instability. Conversely, gentle slopes, sandstone unit, and dense vegetation cover were strongly associated with low-susceptibility regions. papers.title: Beyond Vulnerability: Women’s Water Stewardship and Adaptive Agency in Climate-Vulnerable Bangladesh
papers.summary: Abstract In Bangladesh, the climate crisis manifests through acute water scarcity, which profoundly disrupts social reproduction, particularly for women. Using a Feminist Political Ecology (FPE) lens, this study explores women’s adaptive agency in daily water management practices at both household and community levels. The study was conducted in three climate-vulnerable regions of Bangladesh: Mongla (cyclone-prone coastal Bagerhat), Naogaon (drought-prone), and Cox’s Bazar (flash flood- and landslide-prone). The study employed a qualitative approach incorporating in-depth interviews with women and focus group discussions which complemented by non-participant observation. In addition, key informant interviews were conducted with local government representatives, government officials and NGO staff working on climate change adaptation to understand the institutional setting. Data were thematically analysed following six steps of the thematic analysis process. The results show that women play a crucial role as water stewards, using their traditional knowledge, social networks, and collective action to enhance household and community resilience in the face of climate uncertainty. However, formal governance institutions seldom recognize their contributions. The study therefore recommends that local water governance and the vital role of women’s traditional knowledge be recognized in policies, and that leadership for a gender-responsive adaptation framework to climate change be adopted.

papers.title: Understanding the propagation processes and driving mechanisms of meteorological, hydrological, and agricultural droughts in Xinjiang
papers.summary: Drought propagation among meteorological, hydrological, and agricultural systems poses significant challenges to water security and agricultural sustainability in arid regions. This study investigated the propagation mechanisms and driving factors of multi-type droughts in Xinjiang, China, using ERA5-Land reanalysis data (1990–2024) to derive the standardized precipitation index (SPI), standardized runoff index (SRI), and standardized soil moisture index (SSI). Wavelet coherence analysis (WTC), maximum Pearson correlation coefficient (MPCC), Copula-based modeling, and SHAP analysis were integrated to identify drought propagation pathways, response thresholds, and dominant drivers. Results showed that drought variability decreased with increasing timescales, whereas SSI exhibited stronger persistence, and the coherence among drought types strengthened at medium- and long-term scales. Agricultural drought responded to meteorological drought with an average lag of approximately 4 months, while hydrological drought exhibited delays of 3–7 months, with agricultural-to-hydrological drought propagation occurring after 2–3 months. Propagation thresholds ranged from −1.00 to −1.97 for meteorological-to-hydrological drought, −1.07 to −2.28 for meteorological-to-agricultural drought, and − 1.04 to −2.32 for agricultural-to-hydrological drought. Soil moisture emerged as a key regulator of drought evolution, while precipitation availability, runoff processes, and hydrothermal conditions jointly controlled drought variability and propagation. These findings provide a scientific basis for drought monitoring, early warning, and adaptive water resource management under climate change, supporting agricultural drought mitigation and regional disaster risk reduction. Practical implications This research systematically elucidates the propagation patterns, critical thresholds, and driving mechanisms of drought across meteorological, hydrological, and agricultural systems. papers.title: Causes and impact of the 2081 Flood of Sunkoshi River in Khurkot, Golanjor Rural Municipality, Sindhuli, Nepal
papers.source: Universal Technical Journal of Lumbini International Academy of Science and Technology
papers.summary: Nepal’s steep topography and monsoon-dominated climate make it highly vulnerable to floods and flash floods. In 2081 B.S., a catastrophic flash flood struck Khurkot, at the confluence of the Sunkoshi and Tamakoshi rivers in Golanjor Rural Municipality, Sindhuli, and affected more than 500 families. This study was done to find the natural and human-induced causes of the flood, its socio-economic, infrastructural and environmental impacts, and ways to reduce future risk. A mixed-methods design was used. A household questionnaire survey was carried out with 150 respondents, and 19 problems associated with the flood, together with their causes, effects and mitigation measures, were ranked using the Relative Importance Index (RII). Field observation, a focus group discussion with community members and an in-depth interview with a technical expert of the rural municipality were also carried out. The results show that the biggest problem is weak coordination in disaster response and relief distribution (RII 0.88), followed by destruction of roads and transportation network (RII 0.87), loss of agricultural land and crops (RII 0.86) and riverbank erosion causing land loss (RII 0.85), while illegal riverbed extraction was ranked lowest (RII 0.71). The strongest cause of weak coordination was the absence of a clear inter-agency command and communication protocol (RII 0.83). Heavy monsoon rainfall, uncontrolled extraction of sand and gravel, removal of riverbank vegetation and inadequate flood protection structures were found to be important causes behind many of the impacts. Field observation showed that nearly 90 percent of the cultivated land in the affected belt was inundated, buried or swept away. The study suggests a single disaster coordination authority, stronger embankments and flood-resilient roads and bridges, better drainage, regulation of riverbed extraction, riverbank bioengineering, and an early warning system with community preparedness training.

papers.title: Permafrost Monitoring in the Arctic Network of National Parklands
papers.summary: Permafrost underlies most of the Arctic Network and affects nearly everything in the arctic ecosystem, from soils and vegetation to water and wildlife. Permafrost is ground that doesn’t thaw in the summer due to a cold climate. Permafrost perches water near the surface, making soils wet and runoff fast. The striking polygonal patterned ground so characteristic of the arctic is due to permafrost. Ice can build up in the ground and then thaw, producing pits, ponds, lakes, and landslides. Many scientists believe that our climate is warming and permafrost will thaw; some think that permafrost thaw has already started. Thaw of permafrost could have many consequences, such as drainage of lakes, creation of new ponds, soil erosion, slumps, siltation of streams and lakes, release of greenhouse gasses, and changes in soil wetness and nutrient supplies. Unravelling landslide susceptibility controls using machine learning and explainable AI in a tropical river basin of the Western Ghats, India
papers.summary: Landslide susceptibility assessment is essential for risk-informed land-use planning in humid tropical river basins, where intense monsoon rainfall, steep terrain and expanding human disturbance interact to destabilise slopes. This study develops an explainable Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) framework for landslide susceptibility mapping in the Manimala River Basin, Kerala, India. A landslide inventory and twelve conditioning factors, including slope, rainfall, topographic wetness index, lineaments, streams, roads, curvature, lithology, soil, and land use/land cover (LU/LC), were used to develop the model. The dataset was divided into training and testing subsets using a 70:30 ratio, and model performance was evaluated using AUROC, precision–recall, and confusion-matrix-based metrics. The LightGBM model showed strong predictive performance, with an AUROC of 0.894 and an average precision of 0.878. Threshold-based validation yielded an accuracy of 0.833, precision of 0.864, sensitivity of 0.792, specificity of 0.875, and an F1-score of 0.826, indicating balanced classification of landslide and non-landslide samples. The susceptibility map revealed that high- and very high-susceptibility zones together occupy 5.69% of the basin, mainly concentrated in the eastern and north-eastern uplands along the Western Ghats, whereas 83.66% of the basin falls under the least susceptible class. SHAP-based explainability identified slope as the dominant control on landslide susceptibility, followed in relative importance by rainfall, topographic wetness index (TWI), and distance to lineaments. The proposed explainable framework provides both accurate susceptibility mapping and transparent geomorphic interpretation for climate-resilient local planning.

papers.title: Climate hazards, water insecurity, and menstrual-health capability deprivation among women and girls in Bangladesh
papers.summary: This dataset contains the R code, variable dictionary, coding notes, supplementary appendix, and aggregate results for the article "Climate hazards, water insecurity, and menstrual-health capability deprivation among women and girls in Bangladesh: a nationally representative, geospatially linked cross-sectional study" (Howlader MH, Moin MMH). The study analyses 61,527 women aged 15–49 years in the 2025 Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS7). An Alkire–Foster index of menstrual-health capability deprivation (seven indicators in four dimensions: material adequacy, privacy and dignity, functional participation, and bodily agency and care access) is related to household-reported climate hazards (flood, drought, cyclone or tidal surge, landslide), drinking-water insufficiency, and hazard-related toilet disruption. Methods include survey-weighted logistic regression, average marginal effects, a negative-control outcome, E-values, and geographic analyses (Moran's I, Getis–Ord Gi* hot spots, Fay–Herriot district estimates, MICS geospatial covariates, coastal-zone effect modification, and spatially smoothed models). Contents: - code/: R scripts (00–06 and run_all.R) that reproduce all tables and figures in the article and supplementary appendix. - data/: instructions for obtaining the input data (data not included). - docs/: supplementary appendix (PDF), variable dictionary, coding notes, and conceptual framework figure. - results/: tables (xlsx), figures (PNG, PDF), district-level estimates (GeoPackage), verification report, and R session information. The MICS7 microdata, cluster GPS coordinates, and geospatial covariates belong to the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics and UNICEF and cannot be redistributed; they are available free of charge to registered users at https://mics.unicef.org/surveys. District boundaries are available at https://data.humdata.org/dataset/cod-ab-bgd. Only aggregate, non-identifiable results are included in this dataset.

papers.title: Comparative Analysis of Geotextile-Reinforced Embankment Slope Stability Using the Bishop Method in GeoStudio SLOPE/W and Finite Element Analysis in PLAXIS 2D: A Case Study of the Klaten–Purwomartani Toll Road Project, Section 1, Package 1.2, STA 38+000
papers.summary: This study aims to analyze the stability of embankment slopes in the Klaten–Purwomartani Toll Road Construction Project Section 1Package 1.2 STA 38+000 by comparing the analysis results using GeoStudio SLOPE/W and PLAXIS 2D, as well as evaluating the effectiveness of geotextile reinforcement and verification using the Bishop method. The research data were obtained from independent laboratory testing of subgrade soil at depths of 1–3 m. The classification results indicate that the subgrade soil is dominated by clay and silt with different shear strength characteristics at each depth, while the embankment material is classified as loamy sand. The analysis without reinforcement shows that increasing embankment height and variations in loading conditions reduce the Safety Factor (SF) value, with the most critical condition occurring at an 8 m embankment height, which does not meet the requirements of SNI 8460:2017 (SF ≥ 1.5). The application of Woven Staple Fiber Polypropylene UNW-60P geotextile reinforcement effectively increases the SF value by approximately 80%, allowing all critical conditions to meet the stability requirements. Verification using the Bishop method produces SF values ranging from 1.626–2.884, all of which satisfy the requirements of SNI 8460:2017. The comparative analysis results show that PLAXIS 2D produces more conservative SF values because it considers stress distribution, deformation, and pore water pressure using the Finite Element Method (FEM) with the Strength Reduction Method (SRM), while GeoStudio SLOPE/W based on the Limit Equilibrium Method (LEM) produces relatively higher SF values and is suitable for preliminary slope stability evaluation.

papers.title: Ecological Indicators Reveal Contrasting Post-Earthquake Recovery Trajectories and Resilience Across Mountain Ecosystems
papers.summary: Net primary productivity (NPP) is a useful ecological indicator for evaluating ecosystem functioning and recovery after natural disturbance. Here, we used multi-source remote-sensing and environmental data from 2010 to 2024 to compare post-earthquake NPP recovery in the 2017 Jiuzhaigou and Milin earthquake regions. We integrated trend analysis, temporal persistence assessment, co-seismic landslide overlay, eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) interpreted using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), and locally weighted scatterplot smoothing (LOWESS)-based contribution-transition detection to compare NPP dynamics and environmental associations in the two earthquake-affected regions. The two regions exhibited contrasting responses. The slope of regional mean annual NPP decreased from 9.69 to 8.21 g C m−2 yr−2 between the pre- and post-earthquake periods in Jiuzhaigou, whereas it increased from 3.69 to 9.37 g C m−2 yr−2 in Milin. Hurst-based trend-persistence analysis indicated a higher proportion of sustained improvement and a lower proportion of degradation-related classes in Jiuzhaigou, whereas Milin showed more degradation-related classes. Within co-seismic landslide zones, sustained degradation dominated in both regions and was more extensive in Milin. XGBoost–SHAP results showed that pre-earthquake NPP was the most influential predictor in both regions, but the contributions of secondary predictors differed. Elevation made a larger relative contribution to the Jiuzhaigou model, whereas pre-earthquake NDVI, precipitation, and temperature made larger relative contributions to the Milin model. LOWESS analysis further revealed distinct nonlinear response transitions in temperature, precipitation, and elevation. These results demonstrate the value of combining NPP trends, temporal persistence, and model interpretation to compare vegetation productivity dynamics and inform assessments of post-earthquake functional recovery in mountain ecosystems.

papers.title: Use of bamboo-based bio-engineering for flood and soil erosion control: a case study of Jhiku Khola, Kavrepalanchok District, Nepal
papers.source: Universal Technical Journal of Lumbini International Academy of Science and Technology
papers.summary: Floods and soil erosion along mid-hill streams severely threaten agricultural land, infrastructure and rural livelihoods across Nepal. While conventional civil engineering structures such as gabions and masonry walls involve high capital and maintenance costs, bamboo-based soil bio-engineering offers a sustainable, nature-based alternative. This study evaluates the application, perceived effectiveness and operational constraints of bamboo bio-engineering along the Jhiku Khola in Panchkhal Municipality, Kavrepalanchok District. Using a mixed-method approach, primary data were gathered between March and August 2020 through a structured questionnaire survey (n = 108) analyzed with the Relative Importance Index (RII), complemented by focus group discussions, key informant interviews and field observations. Floods (RII = 0.77), concentrated in the monsoon, and soil erosion (RII = 0.69) were identified as major hazards, with loss of agricultural land (RII = 0.81) cited as the most serious problem. Although 91% of respondents recognized the utility of bamboo in flood mitigation, only 63% had implemented it, highlighting a critical execution gap. Bamboo bio-engineering was rated highly effective (RII = 0.71) and emerged as the most preferred solution (RII = 0.81), with Bansi, Choya and Nigalo identified as the most suitable local species. The main implementation hurdles were a shortage of technical, site-specific studies and designs, weak inter-governmental coordination and the difficulty of transporting bamboo to the river basin; these are compounded by the absence of municipal rate analysis norms for bio-engineering items and by seasonal constraints on budget release, planting material and labour. The study underscores the need to integrate hybrid bio-engineering, combining gabion or masonry toe protection with vegetative palisades, into local disaster risk reduction plans and public procurement frameworks.

papers.title: Study on problems associated with reactive maintenance of roads: A case of selected highways in Far-Western Nepal
papers.source: Universal Technical Journal of Lumbini International Academy of Science and Technology
papers.summary: Road maintenance in the mid-hills and high hills of far-western Nepal is largely reactive, where interventions are made only after pavements, slopes and drainage structures have already failed. Such practice restores traffic temporarily but increases long-term cost and shortens the service life of roads, and very few studies have been carried out to find its root causes in the region. Hence, this study was conducted with an aim to assess the major problems, causes and effects of reactive maintenance of roads and to draw effective mitigation measures for the Khodpe-Chainpur Highway (NH-64), Satbanjh-Gokuleshwor-Darchula section of Mahakali Highway (NH-66) and Anarkholi-Jhulaghat section of Mid-Hill Highway (NH-03). Primary data were collected through field observation, in-depth interview, focus group discussion and questionnaire survey, whereas secondary data were collected from published journal articles, theses, government databases and annual reports. The data collected from 130 respondents were analyzed in Excel using the Relative Importance Index (RII) for Likert scale questions. The results showed that the major problem is escalating structural and geotechnical failures with the highest RII value of 0.80, followed by destruction of supporting works along the road and emergency cleaning of landslides and rockfalls (RII 0.78). Unmanaged vulnerable and unstable slopes, no maintenance of deformed retaining walls until they collapse, limited budget for periodic maintenance and the practice of awarding contracts to the lowest financial bid were identified as the main causes. Among the effects, cyclical budget exhaustion and repeated maintenance received the highest RII of 0.84, indicating that repeated emergency interventions impose a substantial financial burden on road authorities. Dataset of DInSAR wrapped phase signals for AI-based automated detection and classification of mass movements
papers.summary: Abstract With the growing use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in remote sensing of mass movements, open and suitable datasets for model training and validation are increasingly needed. Although Differential Synthetic Aperture Radar Interferometry (DInSAR) is a widely used technique for studying mass movements, wrapped interferograms remain less exploited, and the importance of geomorphological expertise in their interpretation is not usually emphasised. In this work, we introduce a dataset of DInSAR wrapped phase signals designed to support the development of Deep Learning (DL) models for the automated detection and classification of active slow-moving mass movements. The dataset covers two selected wide areas in the Central European Alps and the Northern Apennines. It contains 4910 expert-annotated DInSAR wrapped phase signals derived from 92 Sentinel-1 interferograms with temporal baselines ranging from 6 days to 1 year, classified into nine distinct landslide and periglacial landform classes after careful geomorphological interpretation. This dataset is expected to support the scientific community in AI-based applications for mass movement research, while also serving as a benchmark for the generation of comparable datasets.

Assessing Natural Hazard Exposure and Demographic Vulnerability in Serbian LSGUs Using FAHP and FMULTIMOORA
papers.summary: Natural hazards increasingly represent a significant challenge to sustainable development, disaster risk reduction, and population wellbeing, particularly in regions affected by adverse demographic trends. This study examines the interaction between natural hazard exposure and demographic vulnerability across 25 Serbian local self-government units (LSGUs) through the integration of Geographic Information Systems (GIS), the Triangular Fuzzy Analytic Hierarchy Process (FAHP), and the Fuzzy MULTIMOORA method. Fifteen indicators were organized into three groups representing natural hazard exposure, hazard exposure within built-up areas, and demographic vulnerability. The hazard-related indicators included flood-prone areas, landslide and rockfall susceptibility, seismic hazard, hail-prone areas, and areas exposed to erosion and torrential floods. The demographic indicators included the shares of people with disabilities, population aged 65 years and over, population without educational attainment, economically inactive population, and elderly single-person households. Criterion weights were determined using Triangular FAHP, while Fuzzy MULTIMOORA was applied to rank LSGUs according to their integrated vulnerability. Additional group-specific Fuzzy MULTIMOORA analyses were conducted separately for each indicator group to identify the principal drivers of vulnerability. The integrated assessment identified Ljubovija, Vladičin Han, and Krupanj as the most vulnerable LSGUs, whereas Lebane, Gadžin Han, and Vladimirci occupied the lowest positions. The group-specific analyses further revealed that municipalities characterized by the highest demographic vulnerability were not necessarily those with the highest integrated vulnerability, emphasizing the importance of interactions among environmental and demographic dimensions of vulnerability. papers.title: Study on the geo-environmental and socio-economic impacts of tunnelling works in fragile Himalayan geology: a case study of Nagdhunga Tunnel, Dahachowk, Nepal
papers.source: Universal Technical Journal of Lumbini International Academy of Science and Technology
papers.summary: Tunnelling in the fragile geological formations of the Nepalese Himalayas presents complex geotechnical, hydrogeological and socio-economic challenges. The Nagdhunga–Sisnekhola Tunnel Road Project, Nepal’s first major highway traffic tunnel, was initiated to bypass the congested Sisnekhola–Thankot loop. However, sub-surface excavation has induced significant ground deformation and hydrological disruptions in overlying settlements. This study evaluates the localized environmental, structural and socio-economic impacts of tunnel construction on the Dahachowk area (Ward No. 1) of Chandragiri Municipality, Kathmandu. Utilizing a mixed-method design, primary empirical data were gathered through a household survey (n = 156) analyzed via the Relative Importance Index (RII), supplemented by field observations of 42 dug wells, 12 key informant interviews and 3 focus group discussions. Structural cracks and building damage emerged as the most severe impact (RII = 0.91), followed closely by slope instability/landslides and the drying of traditional drinking water sources (RII = 0.89). Hydrogeological analysis revealed that sub-surface water drawdown significantly lowered pore water pressure, triggering ground settlement, sinkhole formation (RII = 0.91) and building tilt, particularly along the shallow eastern portal zone. The depletion of natural springs increased financial burdens and disproportionately heightened the water-fetching burden on women and children. Furthermore, the absence of a pre-construction Pre-Condition Survey (PCS) and an inaccessible Grievance Redress Mechanism (GRM) exacerbated community distrust, prompting formal complaints to the project financier (JICA). The study recommends mandatory pre-condition structural surveys, pre-excavation grouting, real-time piezometric monitoring, independent third-party damage assessments and community-managed water supply restoration for future tunnelling projects in Nepal.

papers.title: Pysammos 1.0.0: a discrete-to-continuum transformation Python tool to analyse the rheology of granular materials
papers.summary: Abstract. Granular flow processes involving different interstitial fluids and coupling regimes are widespread in both natural systems (e.g., landslides, rock avalanches, river sediment transport) and industrial applications (e.g., aggregates in concrete manufacturing, powder technology, animal feed). Despite this, the behaviour of complex granular flows is not fully understood. Modelling of granular media through software packages that couple the Discrete Element Method with Computational Fluid Dynamics (DEM-CFD) enables a comprehensive description of granular small-scale mechanics through simulations of particle-particle and particle-fluid interactions at high temporal and spatial resolution. These approaches are pivotal in the development of constitutive models that represent the bulk rheology of granular media. While DEM-CFD simulations provide particle-scale information (e.g., particle velocities and forces), extracting continuum fields requires a discrete-to-continuum (D2C) transformation that applies a mathematical approach termed coarse-graining. Although some DEM software packages include built-in D2C capabilities, others, such as MFiX-DEM, do not. Consequently, users are often required to develop custom D2C workflows or adapt simulation outputs to the requirements of other D2C tools. Hence, we introduce Pysammos, a Python package that performs discrete-to-continuum transformations and is designed to be user-friendly, open-source, and computationally efficient. Pysammos is able to process polydisperse granular mixtures of any particle shape, while also offering the option to analyse different particle phases separately. It post-processes output files from MFiX-DEM software and produces vtkhdf outputs ready for visualisation in ParaView, as well as a more generic h5 format for further data analysis. papers.title: A Pilot Machine-Learning Framework for Cumulative Antecedent Rainfall Threshold in Landslide Assessment Along Jalan Simpang Pulai–Blue Valley, Malaysia
papers.summary: Rainfall-induced landslides along Malaysian highway cut slopes are commonly evaluated using empirical thresholds, with limited consideration of cumulative antecedent rainfall. This study evaluates a machine-learning rainfall threshold for five documented shallow-slope failures along Federal Route FT185 (Jalan Simpang Pulai–Blue Valley), Perak, Malaysia, using 520 site-days of daily rainfall records. Cumulative rainfall was calculated over seven windows (1, 3, 5, 7, 14, 21 and 30 days), together with a short-burst intensity feature and a wet-day count and six classifiers (logistic regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, k-nearest neighbours, a support vector machine and XGBoost) were trained under class-weighted, leave-one-site-out cross-validation. Random Forest achieved the best discrimination (ROC-AUC = 0.817), with 80% sensitivity and 90% specificity. Antecedent rainfall consistently ranked above same-day rainfall, indicating the importance of longer-duration rainfall accumulation in the present dataset. An interpretable two-feature logistic regression boundary (14-day antecedent rainfall vs. same-day rainfall) and Random Forest partial-dependence saturation points (approximately 203, 330 and 447 mm for the 14-, 21- and 30-day windows) were derived and combined into a two-tier watch/warning rainfall-probability threshold. The results provide preliminary, site-specific rainfall thresholds for the investigated corridor within a pilot methodological framework requiring prospective validation with additional independent failure events before operational application.

papers.title: Resilient Residential Architecture in Disaster-Prone Areas of Bangladesh: A Study of Flood and Landslide-Responsive Design Strategies
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Abstract This research paper examines resilient residential architectural strategies for disaster-prone areas of Bangladesh, focusing on flood and landslide risks. The study presents two architectural case studies: a 1254 SFT flood-resilient house and an 828 SFT landslide-resilient building. The research focuses on practical architectural responses, including raised planning, water-management strategies, safety setbacks, a 10 ft hybrid wall, drainage planning, site-responsive design, and disaster-aware residential planning. The projects explore how architectural design can respond to environmental risks while maintaining practical and functional living conditions. The study aims to develop an understanding of practical and affordable architectural approaches that may contribute to safer residential environments in vulnerable areas of Bangladesh.

papers.title: Analysis of amplifying effect of antecedent drought on rainfall-induced shallow landslides
papers.summary: Abstract Rainfall-induced shallow landslides are typically attributed to short-term meteorological triggers such as rainfall intensity and duration. However, the influence of antecedent hydrological conditions, particularly prolonged dry spells, has received limited attention despite their potential to alter soil behavior significantly. This study investigates the role of antecedent dry spells on landslide occurrence in the clay-rich terrains of the eastern Black Sea region of Türkiye. Four intense rainfall events from two study sites were examined. At both sites, the later event followed a prolonged dry period and produced a substantially larger mapped landslide inventory despite lower landslide-day rainfall than the earlier event, which occurred under wetter antecedent conditions. To investigate the mechanisms underlying this behavior and evaluate whether it was evident across the event inventories, we combined mechanistic numerical simulations with a data-driven statistical analysis. Numerical simulations indicate that a configuration representing crack-related hydraulic and mechanical changes enhances infiltration and reduces matric suction, resulting in strength reduction and lower slope stability. Additionally, a Generalized Additive Model incorporating landslide-day precipitation, the 30-day Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI-30), local relief, slope steepness, and aspect reveals that landslides are more likely to occur when intense rainfall coincides with drier antecedent conditions rather than under persistently wet conditions. The model showed consistent discriminatory performance under grouped tenfold cross-validation, with an overall ROC AUC of 0.836 based on combined validation-fold predictions. These findings suggest that in clay-rich environments, conventional rainfall thresholds used in predictive models may underestimate landslide occurrence probability when preceded by dry spells. papers.title: Disaster Severity Weighted GCN-LSTM Routing Framework in Underwater Sensor Networks
papers.source: International Journal of Electrical and Electronics Engineering
papers.summary: The events such as earthquakes, tsunamis and underwater landslides occur; communication reliability becomes a big challenge in Underwater Wireless Sensor Networks (UWSNs). These events lead to a fast change of channels, failure of links, loss of packets and higher power usage, which diminishes the efficiency of the conventional routing protocols. Most of the protocols that are available today are based on the existing network information and do not anticipate link failure in advance. In this context, a novel Graph Convolutional Network-Long Short-Term Memory-Disaster Severity Weighting (GCN-LSTM-DSW) framework is proposed in this work to support reliable and energy-efficient routing in the presence of disasters. The GCN represents spatial relationships between the neighboring sensor nodes, and the LSTM is used to model temporal variations of the RSSI, SNR, traffic load and residual energy. The Disaster Severity Weighting (DSW) mechanism dynamically adjusts routing costs based on the prediction of network conditions and the severity of the disaster so as to identify unstable links early and select suitable paths. The proposed framework was compared with the individual GCN and LSTM models. GCN achieved an MAE of 0.071, RMSE of 0.099, and R² of 0.917, while LSTM achieved an MAE of 0.086, RMSE of 0.121, and R² of 0.891. The performance of GCN-LSTM-DSW was the best with MAE of 0.048, RMSE of 0.067, and R² of 0.958. In the synthetic disaster scenarios, the proposed framework achieved PDR values ranging from 94.0% to 97.5% across different severity levels, an average end-to-end delay of 185 ms, average energy consumption of 0.82 J, a 12.6% improvement in network lifetime, and a 34.8% reduction in route recovery time. The results show the reliability, energy efficiency and resilience enhancement in dynamic underwater disaster environments.

papers.summary: Keralam is globally recognized as a unique biodiversity hotspot, whose rich forests, rivers, wetlands, and coasts form the very foundation of our public safety, water security, and rural economy. To protect our communities from rising climate risks like extreme floods, landslides, and dry-season droughts, traditional species-level conservation must now evolve into proactive, landscape-wide ecosystem protection. This flagship initiative establishes India’s first scientific baseline for Ecosystem-based Adaptation (EbA), providing local Panchayats and state planners with exact spatial intelligence to strengthen natural flood barriers, stabilize landslide-prone slopes, and streamline disaster risk reduction (DRR). By safeguarding natural life-support systems, the framework directly advances Keralam’s Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) while unlocking new economic horizons for local citizens. Through updated Local Biodiversity Action Plans (LBSAPs), local Biodiversity Management Committees (BMCs) and indigenous forest-dwelling communities will be empowered to implement NbS based development, secure sustainable livelihoods—converting high-integrity ecosystem protection into viable revenue streams from blue carbon, blue economy, eco-restoration incentives, carbon credits, and non-timber forest produce (NTFP) trade.

Evaluating pre- and post-failure behavior of a large waste dump by combining LEM and DEM approach: a case study from a hydropower station, China
papers.summary: Large hydropower projects generate extensive waste dumps, posing significant environmental risks. Conventional 2D analyses fail to capture 3D topographic effects of typical gully terrain, while 3D discrete element method (DEM) are suitable but face calibration challenges for post-failure simulations. This study investigates a waste dump at the Yongjia Pumped Storage Power Station, China by integrating (1) a self-developed rigorous 3D Limit Equilibrium Method (LEM) for the pre-failure analysis and (2) a well-calibrated DEM for post-failure behavior. The 3D LEM reveals how meandering topography enhances stability, underscoring 3D analysis necessity. DEM simulations identify the interparticle friction coefficient (μ) as the controlling factor for debris flow trajectories and deposition patterns in winding valleys. A key highlight lies in the qualitative cross-model comparison linking the pre-failure and post-failure analyses, which supports μ = 0.2 as a representative value for the present DEM configuration and the engineering scenarios considered. This leads to a local mobilized area that remains confined within proximal slopes in DEM simulations, equivalent to a slight stability margin in LEM from the same local topographic constraints. However, failure risks persist under extreme conditions (e.g., drainage failure), where strength parameter uncertainties may arise from inadequate compaction or water lubrication (further reducing μ). Our cross-model results suggest specific reinforcement strategies to reduce the downstream risk.

papers.title: Cambio de Uso del Suelo y Vulnerabilidad Ante Riesgos Naturales en Regiones Montañosas
papers.source: Ibero Ciencias - Revista Científica y Académica
papers.summary: Land use change is one of the main processes of environmental transformation and a key driver of ecosystem alteration and of increasing natural hazards, particularly in mountainous regions. The aim of this article was to compile and organize the scientific literature on land use change and natural hazards in mountainous regions. The reviewed evidence shows that agricultural expansion, urbanization, deforestation, and other anthropogenic activities modify land cover, alter hydrological processes, and promote soil degradation, thereby increasing vulnerability to landslides and floods. Furthermore, Geographic Information Systems (GIS) are highlighted as essential tools for analyzing land use change, identifying areas susceptible to natural hazards, and supporting decision-making in territorial management. It is concluded that land use planning grounded in geospatial information and sustainable soil management criteria is essential to reduce vulnerability, strengthen ecosystem resilience, and promote sustainable territorial development.

papers.title: Fractal and multifractal characteristics of particle-size distributions in debris-flow deposits
papers.summary: Particle-size distribution is a fundamental characteristic of debris-flow deposits and provides important information on sediment transport, sorting, and depositional processes. This study investigates ten debris-flow deposit profiles along the sampled main-channel reach along Jiangjiagou, Yunnan Province, China. Mechanical sieving combined with laser diffraction was employed to obtain high-resolution particle-size data, and single-fractal and multifractal approaches were used to quantitatively characterize the spatial variability, structural complexity, and multiscale heterogeneity of particle-size distributions. The results reveal that the deposits were dominated by the coarse fraction (> 0.05 mm), which accounted for 95.75–99.82% of the total particle-size composition, whereas clay and silt contents varied among sampling sites, indicating clear spatial differentiation in particle-size organization. The global fractal dimension ranges from 2.09 to 2.40, reflecting substantial variability in particle mixing and granulometric complexity. The generalized dimension spectra exhibit a typical inverted S-shaped pattern, while D₀, D₁, and D₂ show marked spatial variations among sampling sites. The characteristic singularity strength (α₀) ranges from 0.768 to 1.714, and the spectrum width (Δα) varies from 1.19 to 2.49. D₁/D₀ values are consistently well below unity, further indicating pronounced heterogeneity and multiscale variability in particle-size distributions. Correlation analysis shows that the fractal and multifractal characteristics are closely related to particle-size composition, with fine-particle enrichment generally associated with higher granulometric complexity, whereas coarser deposits tend to exhibit relatively simplified fractal structures. papers.summary: Performance evaluation increasingly informs policy learning and accountability in complex socio-ecological systems (SES). However, when efficiency-based tools are applied to SES, evaluation outcomes are shaped not only by observed performance but also by evaluation-design assumptions. In particular, whether environmental shocks are treated as controllable or uncontrollable influences judgments of performance and responsibility. This study examines how alternative treatments of environmental risk affect SES evaluation outcomes. Using Indonesian provinces as a disaster-prone, environmentally heterogeneous case, we compare a conventional CCR DEA model, a super-efficiency data envelopment analysis (DEA) model, and an enhanced super-efficiency DEA model treating floods and landslides as uncontrollable outputs. The results show that treating environmental risks as uncontrollable substantially changes performance assessments, rankings, and responsibility attribution. By reframing SES efficiency analysis as an evaluation-design problem rather than a technical exercise, this study demonstrates how controllability assumptions shape evaluation outcomes and provides transferable insights for designing fair, transparent evaluations in complex SES.

papers.summary: Groundwater is often a primary source of freshwater in many parts of the world. Fetam River Catchment is among the major river catchments in Ethiopia’s Upper Blue Nile River Basin, where groundwater is a primary source of freshwater. Seasonal rainfall fluctuations, climate, and anthropogenic factors strongly influence the quantity and quality of surface water. Therefore, estimating groundwater recharge is essential for understanding aquifer dynamics and provides a critical basis for sustainable groundwater management. The main aim of the investigation is to estimate the amount of water recharged to the aquifer using the soil moisture balance and Baseflow separation methods in the Fetam River Catchment, and to determine water management thresholds for sustainable development. Fifteen years of River flow data and ten years of daily meteorological data have been used for Baseflow separation and daily soil moisture balance, respectively. Daily soil moisture data analysis yielded a recharge rate of 253.1 ± 78 mm/year, and time-series baseflow data yielded a recharge rate of 187.5 ± 13.23 mm/year. Therefore, the average recharge rate of the catchment based on the two recharge estimation techniques is 220 ± 45.6 mm/year, a sufficient renewable resource. Despite the effects of numerous factors, Baseflow resulted in an underestimation, and the soil moisture balance is overestimated in the investigated area compared to the average of the two techniques. Therefore, the recharge value for river catchments under similar geographical and meteorological circumstances is better estimated by the average of all methods than by any individual technique.

papers.title: Knowledge-guided LLM-GIS framework for relative landslide risk screening and risk-informed management in Hong Kong
papers.summary: This study proposes a large language model and geographic information system (LLM-GIS) framework for quantitative risk assessment (QRA)-inspired relative landslide risk screening and management prioritisation in Hong Kong. Hazard (H), exposure (E), and vulnerability (V) factors were integrated with prior knowledge from documents and relevant studies to develop two LLM reasoning modes. Mode A generated interpretable H-E-V formulations under predefined engineering constraints, whereas Mode B derived sample-wise factor contributions and converted them into regional screening weights. Structured prompts, objective output checks, human review, and deterministic GIS implementation were adopted to improve transparency and auditability. Results show that Mode A achieved an occurrence-consistency AUC of 0.861, compared with 0.782 for Mode B. Sensitivity analysis showed that the vulnerability exponent exerted the strongest influence on the Mode A formulation, while Mode B progressively shifted more weight towards hazard during sequential refinement. SHAP analysis of the final deterministic formulations indicated important contributions from socio-economic vulnerability and terrain-related factors. The risk maps in a case study of Hong Kong provide a regional prioritisation layer for investigation, monitoring, mitigation assessment, and preparedness.

papers.summary: This study aims to analyze the implementation of the Search and Rescue (SAR) team operational policy in handling victims buried by landslides in a tin mining area in Pemali District, Bangka Regency, as well as to identify supporting and inhibiting factors. This study employed a qualitative approach using a case study method. Data were collected through interviews, observation, and documentation involving informants engaged in the SAR operation. The analysis applied George C. Edward III’s policy implementation theory, which consists of communication, resources, disposition, and bureaucratic structure. The results indicate that the implementation of the SAR operational policy generally proceeded well. Communication was supported by interagency coordination, briefings, debriefings, and communication media. Resources included personnel, equipment, and support from various SAR elements. Disposition was reflected in commitment, discipline, responsibility, and compliance with standard operating procedures. The bureaucratic structure operated through a clear command system and division of tasks. Inhibiting factors included unstable terrain, muddy material, secondary landslide risks, and limited communication coverage.

papers.title: Challenges in reconstructing seasonally driven landslide motion from optical satellite data: insights from the Del Medio catchment, NW Argentina
papers.summary: Abstract. Optical satellite images are a valuable resource for studying slow-moving landslides from space. However, monitoring displacement through pairwise image correlation and time-series inversion presents several challenges, including the impact of seasonality on measurement accuracy. Seasonal biases arise from systematic measurement errors related to variable illumination conditions and shadows. These errors manifest in the form of an oscillation pattern in the satellite-derived time series. This complicates the identification of a true seasonal component linked to feedback mechanisms between landslide displacement and a seasonally variable climate. Here, we provide a comprehensive evaluation of different strategies to reduce the magnitude of seasonal biases. These include modeling the seasonal error component, restricting correlation to pairs with similar illumination, weighting, and upsampling optical images. We find that all methods can reduce the impact of systematic seasonal bias at different trade-offs: longer processing times, creation of sparse or disconnected networks, dependence on topographic data, or potential alteration of the true displacement signal. We evaluated the removal of seasonal bias from displacement time series derived from optical satellite data (Landsat-8, Sentinel-2, PlanetScope) over a large slow-moving landslide in the Río Del Medio catchment in northwest Argentina. The transition zone between the Altiplano-Puna plateau and the Andean foreland is characterized by a highly seasonal climate, with intense rainfall during the South American summer monsoon and semi-arid conditions throughout the rest of the year. Over the 10-year observation period, the landslide accumulated approximately 35 m of displacement at spatially and temporally variable rates. papers.title: Landslide Movement Detection Using DInSAR and Sentinel-1A Imagery in a Tropical Volcanic Highland
papers.source: RSF Conference Series Engineering and Technology
papers.summary: Landslides are major geological hazards in tropical mountainous regions, where steep topography, weathered materials, geological structures, and rainfall promote slope instability. This study evaluates Differential Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (DInSAR) to detect and quantify post-landslide surface deformation in a tropical volcanic highland affected by a catastrophic landslide in December 2014. A single Sentinel-1A interferometric pair acquired on 4 August 2017 and 1 May 2026 from the same ascending relative orbit was processed using a standard DInSAR workflow. Line-of-Sight (LOS) displacement was interpreted with geological and geomorphological data. Results show LOS displacement of −0.69 to −0.40 m accumulated over 8.74 years (3,192 days), equivalent to an interval-average rate of approximately 46–79 mm/year. The displacement is spatially associated with structurally controlled volcanic terrain, weathered lithologies, fault and joint systems, and slopes of 30–40%. This study quantifies post-2014 deformation at Telagalele using DInSAR. However, the estimates derive from a single 8.74-year interferometric pair without independent validation and should therefore be interpreted cautiously. The findings indicate DInSAR's potential for post-landslide deformation assessment in tropical mountainous environments.

papers.title: The reactivation of the Niscemi landslide (southern Italy) after the Cyclone Harry
papers.summary: Abstract On January 25, 2026, a large compound slide affected the southern and western slopes of the Niscemi mesa (SE Sicily), causing severe damage to settlements and the evacuation of approximately 1500 people. The event occurred approximately one week after Cyclone Harry, which brought intense rainfall over southern Sicily, and represents the latest reactivation within a historically unstable slope system previously affected by major failures in 1790 and 1997. This study integrates geomorphological mapping, DInSAR and feature-tracking analysis, slope stability modelling, and meteorological data analysis to gain initial insights into the failure mechanisms, precursory and ongoing kinematics, and triggering conditions of the last reactivation of the Niscemi landslide. Results highlight a deep-seated compound mechanism controlled by weak layers and pre-existing slip surfaces within the clayey Mt. San Giorgio Formation. Pre-event interferometric data show limited accelerating deformation at the mesa edge, suggesting rapid failure onset. Numerical simulations suggest the key role of weak layers in governing large-scale instability. The findings emphasize the importance of combining geomorphological memory and satellite data for an improved hazard assessment of dormant landslides that frequently involve slopes of the Apennine Mountains of Italy.

papers.title: Landslide Susceptibility Mapping Using GIS-Based Analytical Hierarchy Process in Pejawaran District, Banjarnegara

papers.summary: Landslide susceptibility mapping is an important tool for identifying relatively unstable zones and facilitating disaster mitigation and land-use planning. This study assesses landslide susceptibility in Pejawaran District, Banjarnegara, Central Java, Indonesia, using a GIS-based Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP). Six conditioning factors were integrated: distance to road, normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI), distance to stream, lithology, elevation, and slope. Pairwise comparison was used to assess the relative importance of these factors. The resulting weights were: distance to road (28%), NDVI (22%), distance to stream (17%), lithology (14%), elevation (10%), and slope (9%). The final landslide susceptibility map was created by combining the weighted thematic layers in a GIS environment. The 54.02 km² study area was classified into five susceptibility levels: very low (8%), low (19%), moderate (28%), high (28%), and very high (16%). High- to very-high-susceptibility areas are mainly concentrated in the central, northern, and eastern parts of the study area, while the western and southwestern sectors generally show lower susceptibility. The spatial distribution of the landslide inventory closely matches the moderate-to-high susceptibility zones. These results indicate that the GIS-AHP approach provides a practical preliminary framework for identifying landslide-prone areas in Pejawaran District.

Development of a Community-Based Anticipatory Action Protocol for Landslide Early Warning Systems
papers.source: RSF Conference Series Engineering and Technology
papers.summary: Landslides pose significant risks to communities in Jombang Regency, East Java, particularly under prolonged rainfall. This study developed an operational anticipatory action protocol that integrates an Internet of Things (IoT)-based landslide early warning system with community observations and multi-channel risk communication in Jumok Hamlet, Sambirejo Village. The study used a community-based approach through a focus group discussion (FGD) with 30 purposively selected participants, field and geological surveys, protocol development, and qualitative validation by experts and community users. The protocol was structured around community-based early warning principles and translated hazard information into four graduated levels: Normal, Advisory, Watch, and Warning. The resulting protocol combines daily rainfall above 61 mm, three-day cumulative rainfall above 91 mm, ground movement above 2 cm/day, progressive crack widening, and soil saturation as operational indicators. The FGD identified widening ground cracks, prolonged rainfall, increasing soil saturation, unusual ground movement, and standing water during soil cultivation as locally recognized warning signs. Expert validation focused on information flow, operational procedures, and stakeholder coordination; user validation focused on SOP readability and usability. Feedback led to clearer trigger-to-action sequences and simpler, context-specific wording. The protocol has not yet been tested during actual landslide events. It links hazard indicators with predefined communication channels and anticipatory actions, including drainage management, mobilization of vulnerable groups, evacuation preparation, and self-evacuation. The study demonstrates how technological monitoring and locally observed indicators can be combined to translate warnings into coordinated community action.

papers.title: Vegetation-Based Early Warning System for Post-Mining Reclamation to Reduce Disaster Risk and Achieve SDGs
papers.source: RSF Conference Series Engineering and Technology
papers.summary: Post-mining land reclamation in Indonesia faces critical operational challenges, particularly in continuously monitoring long-term vegetation recovery trajectories and proactively preventing slope failures and landslide disasters across expansive, remote concession areas. Traditional field-based monitoring protocols are often constrained by high labor costs, limited spatial coverage, and severe logistical difficulties, making the early detection of localized land degradation difficult. To address these limitations, this study develops and evaluates an operational vegetation-based early-warning framework designed to optimize post-mining land management and directly align with Indonesia's commitment to Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)—specifically SDG 15 (Life on Land), SDG 13 (Climate Action), and SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production). The proposed system utilizes multitemporal Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and Soil Adjusted Vegetation Index (SAVI) time series derived from quarterly Sentinel-2 Level-2A satellite imagery. These remote sensing spectral indices were integrated with key contextual attributes, including detailed planting-age datasets and topographic parameters derived from Digital Elevation Models (DEMs), such as slope steepness and elevation profiles. This feature space was subsequently used to train a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) neural network classifier using 462 ground-verified sample pixels collected from an active post-mining reclamation site in Central Sulawesi, Indonesia. The MLP classification model achieved a robust 76% overall predictive accuracy across all designated reclamation status categories. Crucially for disaster risk reduction applications, the model showed exceptional sensitivity to high-risk degradation zones, achieving 98% recall in identifying areas vulnerable to canopy loss, vegetation stress, and potential geotechnical slope instability. papers.summary: Abstract. Ground motion poses a significant threat to the safety and functionality of transport infrastructure, particularly in regions affected by landslides, subsidence, freeze–thaw processes, and large-scale tunnelling. Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) enables millimeter-level displacement monitoring over large areas and is used to support infrastructure risk assessment. Here, we evaluate the usability of two InSAR approaches, (i) Persistent Scatterer Interferometry (PSI) using displacement products from the European Ground Motion Service (EGMS), and (ii) a combined Persistent- and Distributed-Scatterer (PS+DS) phase-linking workflow across key Swedish transport corridors. Rather than a strictly controlled methodological comparison, we evaluate how differences between operational InSAR solutions translate into practical performance for infrastructure monitoring. Results show that PS+DS consistently yields five times as many measurement points while maintaining RMSE values within a similar range to EGMS (mostly below 6 mm in the Line Of Sight direction). The EGMS exhibits narrower RMSE distributions, but PS+DS achieves comparable median RMSE of the measurement points across most land-cover types and corridor environments. Both datasets capture similar displacement patterns along all corridors, with measurement points from both approaches concentrating within the linear corridor geometry. Overall, the five-fold increase in PS+DS point density offers infrastructure operators a practical pathway to finer-scale ground motion monitoring for railway maintenance and risk assessment, while demonstrating how the choice of operational InSAR processing strategy shapes the information available for Earth-observation-based infrastructure applications.

Modeling the Effect of Root Depth and Location on the Stability of Slopes
papers.summary: Vegetation is crucial in maintaining slope stability by preventing soil erosion, landslides, and therefore, safeguarding infrastructure from damage. Several previous studies have shown that vegetation can help to increase slope stability through its mechanical and hydrological effects. This chapter focuses on the mechanical effects of roots on the stability of slope, whereby the effects of root depth and root location were evaluated on 5 and 10-m high slopes. A parametric study was conducted using a numerical model based on limit equilibrium analysis, and a total of 52 numerical simulations were performed. The results revealed that the highest Factor of Safety (FoS) was achieved when the slope was entirely covered with vegetation and the root had the deepest reach of 2.5 m below the ground surface. It also suggested that a slope with deeper roots tends to develop a deeper slip surface compared to slopes with shallow roots. Moreover, it was found that for all cases, the 5-m high slopes had higher FoS compared to the 10-m high slopes. The findings from this study demonstrated that slope height has the most significant influence on the FoS, followed by the root depth and the root locations.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic controls and sedimentary responses of eddy bars during outburst floods
papers.summary: Catastrophic outburst floods are among the most powerful geomorphic agents on Earth, capable of rapidly reshaping mountain river systems and leaving long-lasting sedimentary records. Along the Yarlung Tsangpo River at the southern margin of the Tibetan Plateau, repeated floods triggered by landslide dam or glacial lake failures have produced large eddy bars that preserve information on flood dynamics. However, the hydrodynamic processes linking unsteady flow behavior, vortex activity, and sedimentary responses within flow separation zones remain poorly understood. Here, we reconstructed two Holocene outburst flood events by integrating two-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations with field observations of eddy bars and high-water marks, allowing comparison with the observed geomorphic evidence. Model results indicate that bed shear stresses within flow separation zones commonly exceed entrainment thresholds for coarse sand and fine gravel, allowing sustained near-bed suspension and efficient sediment transport. Under such energetic conditions, the power spectral densities of velocity at the flow separation points, along the separated shear layer, and within the interior of the flow separation zones exhibit broadband and aperiodic behavior with approximate inertial-subrange scaling. These spectral features indicate turbulence-like, multi-scale flow fluctuations associated with unsteady vortex activity during outburst flooding. These fluctuations reflect dynamically evolving vortex configurations, including relatively stable single-vortex systems and more transient multi-vortex systems characterized by splitting, merging, and decay. papers.source: Global and earth surface processes change.
papers.summary: Against the backdrop of global climate change and the increasing frequency of extreme rainfall events, rainfall-triggered clustered landslides have become a major concern in mountainous disaster risk management due to their sudden occurrence, regional clustering, and high destructive potential. This paper systematically reviews the current development and technological advances in early warning models for rainfall-triggered clustered landslides. Particular emphasis is placed on the theoretical foundations and application characteristics of rainfall threshold models, hydrological and physically based models, data-driven models, and physics–data-driven coupled models. The critical role of multi-source monitoring technologies in regional landslide early warning systems is also examined. The review indicates that empirical statistical threshold models, characterized by high computational efficiency and ease of implementation, remain an important approach for rapid risk screening over large areas. Physically based models can capture the underlying relationships among rainfall infiltration, pore-water pressure evolution, and slope failure, but their applications are constrained by the availability of model parameters and computational efficiency.
