papers.title: A prototype multi-hazard early warning system integrating flood and landslide forecasting: application in the upper Garonne River Basin
papers.summary: Multi-Hazard Early Warning Systems (MHEWS) are essential for disaster risk management, yet operational implementation remains limited by challenges in hazard integration, forecast uncertainty, and computational requirements. This study develops and evaluates a fast and lightweight prototype MHEWS integrating fluvial flooding and shallow landslide forecasting. The MHEWS couples snow-hydrological modeling (SNOW-17 and CREST) with a slope stability approach (infinite slope and Random Forest models) driven by bias-corrected Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) meteorological forecasts. Quantile mapping bias correction substantially improves precipitation and temperature forecast performance, reducing variability errors and enhancing distributional agreement. Applied in the Upper Garonne River Basin (Spanish Pyrenees) using 24-hour lead time forecasts, multi-hazard analysis for 2010–2020 reveals asymmetric coupling between hazards: flood warnings respond rapidly to rainfall intensity, while landslide warnings depend on cumulative subsurface conditioning and antecedent soil moisture, with high-level warnings rarely coinciding. Evaluation of multiple forecast lead times (24, 48, 72 h) for June 2013 demonstrates systematic performance degradation with increasing lead time, reflecting amplified uncertainty propagation. This degradation is further compounded by the limitations of the quantile mapping approach; while it effectively aligns marginal statistics, it fails to preserve temporal autocorrelation or event persistence. This introduces residual biases in cumulative dynamics that disproportionately affect landslide prediction compared to flood estimation. The fully automated prototype, designed to be scalable and transferable, and built on open-source software and cloud infrastructure, demonstrates operational feasibility for real-time early warning applications across hydro-meteorologically complex environments.

papers.title: Landslide Susceptibility Assessment in Jinning District, Kunming City, Yunnan Province Based on Multi-Model Comparison
papers.source: Frontiers in Computing and Intelligent Systems
papers.summary: Landslides occur frequently in Jinning District of Kunming City, Yunnan Province, where complex geological conditions make susceptibility assessment a challenging task. In this study, 13 evaluation factors were selected and five machine learning models—Support Vector Machine (SVM), eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGB), Decision Tree (DT), Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), and Random Forest (RF)—were applied to map landslide susceptibility. Pearson correlation coefficients were calculated to examine the relationships among factors, and model performance was compared using AUC, Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-Score, and MCC. The susceptibility maps were then divided into five classes so that the area and landslide proportions of each zone could be compared. Among the five models, XGB achieved the best overall performance, with an AUC of 0.9106 and an MCC of 0.6059. Its very high susceptibility zone covers 13.07% of the study area yet contains 52.33% of the recorded landslides, a concentration that no other model matched. Elevation, slope, and distance to rivers were positively correlated with susceptibility and can be regarded as the dominant controlling factors. These findings offer a scientific reference for landslide risk management in Jinning District and confirm that machine learning models are effective for geological disaster susceptibility assessment.

papers.title: Psychosocial impact of natural disasters in a rural Himalayan community: A qualitative study
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Background: The Himalayan region is highly vulnerable to disasters such as landslides, cloudbursts, and flash floods. Difficult terrain and limited resources often delay rescue and recovery efforts, which negatively affect the mental health of affected communities. Aim: To explore the lived experiences, psychological impact, support systems, and perceived needs of disaster-affected communities in Munsyari block, Pithoragarh, Uttarakhand, and to generate context-specific insights to strengthen community-based disaster mental health responses. Materials and Methods: A qualitative design was used, involving three focus group discussions (FGDs) with 6–10 participants each, aged 25–60 years, from Borahabaggad and Dhapa villages. After obtaining verbal consent, discussions lasting 45–60 minutes were recorded, transcribed in the native language, and translated into English. Data were thematically analyzed using Atlas.ti software to support coding and organization. Ethical approval was obtained from the institutional ethics committee. Results: Findings revealed that strong community relationships offered crucial emotional and material support. However, recovery was hindered by financial constraints, inadequate infrastructure, and limited access to formal mental health care. Participants reported dependence on informal support systems and insufficient long-term government assistance. Improved disaster preparedness and locally grounded support were identified as key needs. Conclusion: The study concludes that while community networks play a vital role, they are inadequate to address the full spectrum of survivors’ needs. Integrating mental health into disaster response and strengthening community-based preparedness can enhance resilience and mitigate long-term psychological impacts.

papers.title: Efficient High-Resolution Mapping of Small Groundwater Seeps Along an Intermittent Stream Using Thermal Infrared and Hydrochemical Techniques
papers.summary: Localized groundwater inflow can create spatial heterogeneity in intermittent stream discharge, temperature, and chemistry. However, locations and physicochemical properties of the groundwater inflow often remain poorly investigated at the reach and sub-reach scale. Here, we combined high-resolution mapping of groundwater seeps using thermal infrared (TIR) imaging with longitudinal electric conductivity (EC) and discharge measurements to efficiently reveal this heterogeneity with a short, targeted field campaign. At the transition to the dry summer season (early July), we mapped water temperatures and identified any seeps in the TIR images along a 341-m stream reach of the semi-arid Gibson Jack Creek, Idaho. We then measured the stream/seep ECs and longitudinal changes in stream discharge along the reach. Along the reach, the one-day TIR survey effectively mapped 27 previously unidentified small seeps that lacked distinct topographic features. Although the geological map reveals consistent geology along the entire reach – landslide deposit on the left bank and limestone on the right bank – the seep water characteristics abruptly change at 125 m along the reach. On average, the temperature and EC were 1.3°C lower and 1.7 times higher, respectively, downstream of the 125 m breakpoint than upstream of this point. Salt dilution gauging showed that seep water contributions increased the downstream stream discharge by fivefold relative to upstream of the breakpoint (104 m), and this pattern was independently supported by two-source separation analyses based on temperature and EC. Our findings demonstrate that a seemingly homogeneous stream reach can contain hydrologically distinct groundwater sources that strongly control longitudinal patterns of intermittent stream discharge, temperature, and chemistry. This highlights the importance of integrating point-scale characterization of groundwater inputs with reach-scale assessments of intermittent streams.

It integrates Large Language Models (LLMs), Multi-Agent RAG, Digital Twins, GIS, IoT, CCTV, UAVs, and satellite data to provide accurate situational awareness. Specialized AI agents analyze real-time information to identify risks, affected areas, and resource requirements. The Agentic RAG system retrieves relevant historical data, emergency procedures, maps, and disaster knowledge to support decision-making. The framework generates adaptive, evidence-based response strategies for rescue prioritization, resource allocation, evacuation, and emergency coordination.

papers.title: Analisis pergerakan lereng tambang menggunakan alat ssr (slope stability radar) pit kgu pt cipta kridatama jobsite pt borneo indobara di kabupaten tanah bumbu provinsi kalimantan selatan
papers.summary: Mine slopes play a vital role in mining operations, making slope stability one of the most critical geotechnical challenges in the mining industry. Careful slope design is essential to ensure operational safety; however, continuous monitoring remains necessary because stable slopes may become unstable due to ground movement that can eventually trigger slope failure. One of the most advanced monitoring technologies is the GroundProbe Slope Stability Radar (SSR-XT), a ground-based radar system capable of measuring displacement with an accuracy of up to 0.04 mm. Its rapid, real-time data acquisition enables early detection of slope deformation and potential failures.This study was conducted at PT Cipta Kridatma in the PIT KGU area using SSR monitoring data from pixel coordinates x = 65, y = 26 and x = 167, y = 25 during January 2026. The observed deformation behavior was predominantly linear, with several regressive deformation events and one progressive deformation event that resulted in a slope failure on January 28, 2026, at 13:38. Failure prediction was performed using the inverse velocity method with MonitorIQ and Microsoft Excel. Back-analysis estimated the failure time at 14:28. Before failure, the monitored slope recorded a cumulative displacement of 627 mm and a velocity of 8.44 mm/hour. The failure covered approximately 2,164 m², with an estimated volume of 21,641 m³ and mass of 56,267 tons. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of SSR monitoring and the inverse velocity method for improving slope failure prediction and geotechnical risk management.

papers.title: Stationary Susceptibility and Dynamic Landslide Hazard Forecasting System for Georgia Using ERA5, Fuzzy Logic, and Hybrid Machine Learning
papers.summary: Georgia, due to its high mountains, growth of population, intensive land use, and the number of vulnerable infrastructures (roads, large engineering constructions, etc.), as well as climate change, belongs to the one of most vulnerable regions in the world, as it is prone to hazardous geological processes such as landslides (LSs). As the statistical data on LSs in Georgia are of low quality, due to political turmoils in the first decades of XXI-th century, a three-stage methodology was applied for assessing LS susceptibility. On the first stage, we perform the initial statistical assessment of LS susceptibility, using 11 weighted objective factors analysis. Then the machine learning (ML) methods were used for obtaining the final map of LS susceptibility. In conditions of Georgia, the intensive and prolonged precipitation is one of the main triggering factors for activation of LS processes. Therefore, in this study we also use hourly precipitation data, meteorological station observations, a historical landslide catalogue and hybrid machine learning approaches to construct spatial-temporal LS hazard maps under 24 h, 3-day, 5-day, and 30-day cumulative precipitation conditions. Predictive performance was evaluated retrospectively using a balanced sample of 309 landslide events and 309 susceptibility-matched controls, including a temporal train–test split. The results characterize discrimination under this sampling design; performance at the natural frequency of landslides requires independent evaluation. The results obtained show that the acceleration of global warming in recent decades affects the assessment of LS susceptibility/hazard.

Remote Sensing-based Integration of Land Use/Land Cover, Vegetation Cover, and Land Surface Temperature with Hydrological Implications in Tikrit City, Iraq
papers.summary: This study examines the integrated relationship among Land Use/Land Cover (LULC), Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), and Land Surface Temperature (LST), with hydrological implications, in Tikrit City, Iraq, using Landsat data acquired in 2017 and 2025. LULC, NDVI, and LST layers were prepared using the same spatial boundary, and 4124 paired sample points were extracted from identical locations to support temporal and statistical comparison. The LULC results showed a clear reduction in Soil from 70.52% in 2017 to 49.88% in 2025, whereas Vegetation increased from 25.49% to 44.12%. Built Area also increased from 3.08% to 4.90%, indicating moderate urban expansion. The dominant land-cover transition was from Soil to Vegetation, covering 66,014.66 ha. Mean NDVI increased significantly from 0.061 to 0.075, while mean LST remained statistically stable, changing only from 41.992°C to 42.031°C. However, non-parametric tests indicated that the spatial distribution of LST changed significantly. The NDVI–LST relationship was positive in both years, with Pearson correlation increasing from 0.670 in 2017 to 0.709 in 2025. Regression analysis showed that NDVI explained 44.9% and 50.2% of LST variation in 2017 and 2025, respectively. Class-based analysis indicated that the dominant heat-contributing class shifted from Soil in 2017 to Built Area in 2025. These findings show that surface thermal behavior in Tikrit City cannot be explained by vegetation cover alone, but depends on land-cover composition, mixed pixels, agricultural activity, soil exposure, surface moisture, and seasonal conditions. From a hydrological perspective, the reduction of exposed soil, expansion of vegetation, and growth of built-up areas have implications for infiltration opportunity, runoff potential, evapotranspiration tendency, and surface moisture retention.

papers.summary: This paper presents an automated, cloud-native geospatial Decision Support System (DSS) that generates variable rate prescription maps directly from Sentinel-2 satellite observations. Designed as an end-to-end arable field VRA architecture, the system operates completely autonomously with minimal input, requiring only the field boundary polygon, the crop phenology class (winter or spring crop), and the multi-year observation window. Instead of the rapidly saturating Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), the model relies on the Normalized Difference Red Edge (NDRE) index, which accurately captures canopy chlorophyll and green biomass dynamics. For each native 10×10 m grid cell, the system extracts the 95th percentile (P95) peak value within a crop-specific reproductive phenological window, eliminating single-day snapshot noise while validating winter or spring growth trajectories via automated phenological ratio calculations. papers.title: Drought responses of a Norway spruce forest on drained peat soil: combining sap-flow sensors, eddy-covariance, meteorological, soil and UAV data
papers.summary: Abstract. The summer of 2021 brought a severe drought to southern Finland. We explored how a drained boreal peatland forest responds to drought by combining a wide range of in situ monitoring and Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) remote sensing. A dataset combining eddy-covariance (EC) fluxes, sap-flow sensors, UAV mapping, soil and weather data was collected. Spruce stand reaction to drought is examined at sub-daily to seasonal time scales, and its temporal and spatial features are identified separately for a recently thinned Continuous Cover Forestry (CCF) block and a control block. Sap flow data showed that the CCF-harvested block shows greater tree resilience to high vapour pressure deficit (VPD) than the control block, likely due to the higher soil water availability during the rainless and hot period. At the same time, both the control and CCF harvest blocks had notably reduced net ecosystem exchange (NEE) and increased Bowen ratio, particularly on high VPD days. The UAV surveys indicated that trees in the CCF block tend to have higher canopy temperatures and lower Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) than in the control block, implying their possible susceptibility to more extreme drought.

Self-Catalyzed Hastelloy Fiber Paper (HAP) Porous Transport Layer for Oxygen Evolution Reaction in Anion Exchange Membrane Water Electrolysis
papers.summary: Abstract Hastelloy fiber paper (HAP) can be used as the oxygen evolution reaction porous transport layer (PTL) without using a catalyst layer in anion exchange membrane water electrolysis. It is combined with Ru on nickel fiber paper (NFP) (hydrogen evolution reaction PTL) to form an asymmetric Ru/NFP(−)//HAP(+) single-cell system. The experimental results for electrodeposited Co(OH)2 on HAP are also demonstrated for comparison. At 70 °C, the cell delivers 725.67 mA cm–2 at 1.8 V under cathode-wet conditions and maintains 701.34 mA cm–2 under cathode-dry operation. A 5000-cycle accelerated stress test (AST) confirms the good operational stability of the system under dynamic cycling conditions. In addition, the effect of Co(OH)2 electrodeposition on the HAP anode was further investigated to show the current density decreases to 485.59 mA cm–2 at 1.8 V when operated at 70 °C. The AST stability also degrades with Co(OH)2 deposition. Further analysis indicates that the electrodeposited Co(OH)2 coating may alter the pore structure and surface wettability of the catalyst layer, leading to mass-transport limitations at high current densities, including hindered ion transport and inefficient oxygen bubble removal.

papers.summary: Groundwater-level fluctuations can induce differential deformation at ground-fissure sites, yet systematic experimental investigations of hydraulic and layered deformation responses across fissures during pumping-recharge remain limited. Under the present experimental conditions, hydraulic and deformation responses varied markedly among different layers and between the two sides of the fissure. Enhancing the Surface Characteristics of Coal Gangue through Different Modification Methods and the Improvement of Saline-Alkali Soil
papers.summary: Abstract Coal gangue exhibits great application potential in saline-alkali soil amelioration. However, natural coal gangue has a limited improvement effect due to its small specific surface area and poor surface activity. In this study, different modification methods were employed to improve the surface properties of coal gangue. Changes in the surface properties of modified coal gangue and their improvement effects in saline-alkali soil were investigated by XRD, FTIR, SEM, static soil culture tests, and simulated leaching tests. Compared with original coal gangue, modified coal gangue shows significantly enhanced active components, in which the stable kaolinite is transformed into active Al2O3 and SiO2 according to XRD analysis. In addition, the micropore structure of modified coal gangue has changed, showing a rougher surface, larger pore diameter and specific surface area. Especially for calcination-modified coal gangue, the specific surface area is greatly increased from 6.9 m2/g to 34.8 m2/g. The application of coal gangue modified by calcination, acid treatment, and ball milling can effectively reduce the pH of saline-alkali soil from 9.89 to 7.99, 8.40, and 8.74, respectively. Meanwhile, their incorporation can reduce the exchangeable sodium content of saline-alkali soil by 36.2%, 33.6%, and 40.7%, respectively. The addition of modified coal gangue has a significant effect on reducing nutrient loss during the leaching of saline-alkali soil. When the amount of calcination-modified coal gangue added reaches 30%, the loss of soil total nitrogen and total phosphorus can be reduced by 94% and 90%, respectively. The results demonstrate that modified coal gangue, owing to its increased active components and surface sites, can not only reduce the pH and exchangeable sodium content of saline-alkali soil, but also effectively mitigate nutrient leaching losses. Integrating machine learning failure probabilities and tracer-based infiltration indicators for sewer condition screening and asset management
papers.summary: Wastewater utilities need transparent decision-support methods to prioritise sewer rehabilitation when CCTV inspection data are incomplete and groundwater infiltration creates operational and environmental burdens. Machine learning (ML) models are being trained on sewer inspection data to perform as modern asset-management tools. However, given the limited availability of inspection data, independent external supporting data that are less resource-intensive to collect would be highly valuable. Tracer-based infiltration estimates are one such indicator. To our knowledge, this is the first study to combine these two techniques and compare ML-based structural failure probability with independent tracer-based evidence of groundwater infiltration under dry-weather conditions. As infiltration cannot be reliably estimated at the pipe level, we aggregated the studied network into 21 operational zones and estimated infiltration severity using dry-weather tracer data, based on electrical conductivity (EC) and chemical oxygen demand (COD), within a binary mixing framework. In parallel, ML-based condition prediction models were developed using an IPCW-weighted machine-learning framework trained on CCTV inspection data, aggregating the resulting predicted failure probabilities to the zone level using length-weighted averaging. Zones were ranked according to ML-predicted failure probability and tracer-based infiltration severity. The agreement between the two rankings was positive but statistically uncertain (Kendall's τ-b = 0.254-0.305; p = 0.108-0.056; concordance index = 0.628-0.655). Overall, the proposed framework provides a practical cross-evidence screening approach for environmental management and sewer asset-management decision-making when comprehensive inspection data are unavailable.

Diagnosing governance and data gaps in urban groundwater management with a transferable workflow based methodology evidenced in Munich
papers.summary: Abstract Urban groundwater management is emerging as a critical sustainability challenge in European cities under accelerating pressures of climate change and urbanization. Despite substantial investment in monitoring infrastructure and technical expertise, effective groundwater management remains constrained by institutional fragmentation across multiple departments and authorities with dispersed responsibilities, disconnected data systems, and limited coordination. In the two Munich processes examined, the main barrier lay not in technical knowledge, but in institutional governance. The objective of this paper is to develop and demonstrate a methodology that improves the institutional governance of urban groundwater management. The paper applies a four-step Data-Governance Diagnostic combining stakeholder engagement, data assessment, governance workflow analysis, and prioritization of critical gaps, illustrated through two Munich application cases: rainwater infiltration under the Sponge City strategy and thermal groundwater use under the Municipal Heating Plan. Findings show that recurring problems, fragmented data infrastructures, limited digitalization, and data-sharing restrictions, are symptoms of deeper governance weaknesses. Groundwater data can only deliver practical value when embedded in governance systems that enable coordination, accessibility, and effective use in decision-making. The novelty is threefold: a practitioner-friendly step-by-step diagnostic applicable directly by municipalities; a structured output making principal data and governance gaps explicit and actionable; and the demonstration that these gaps are mutually reinforcing and must be addressed simultaneously. Future research should validate the methodology across cities of varying size, institutional capacity, and stage of urban development outside the Alpine context. papers.title: Spatial associations between urbanization, watershed runoff potential, and groundwater-depth change in a Semi-Arid Alluvial Plain, Multan, Pakistan
papers.summary: Groundwater decline in irrigated semi-arid alluvial plains reflects interacting land-surface, climatic, pumping, and hydrogeological controls. This study evaluates spatial associations among urbanization, Curve Number-based event-runoff potential, regional climate variability, and groundwater-depth change in Multan, Pakistan. Thirty-nine wells with pre- and post-monsoon observations for 2005, 2010, 2015, and 2018 were assigned to four watershed groups delineated using an approximately 30-m DEM and HydroBASINS Level-12 topology. Land-use/land-cover maps for 2010, 2015, and 2020, SoilGrids Hydrologic Soil Group data, and regional NASA POWER climate data for 2003–2018 were summarized using the same watershed boundaries. Mean groundwater-depth increases from pre-monsoon 2005 to post-monsoon 2018 were 19.32, 7.21, 5.76, and 15.69 m in Groups 1–4, respectively. Only Group 1 had a 95% confidence interval excluding zero. Urban fraction increased in all groups, while mean Curve Number values remained high and increased modestly by 0.24–0.64. Scenario calculations indicated only modest changes in event runoff. Climate analysis showed modest spatial rainfall variability, no significant trends in precipitation, temperature, or reference evapotranspiration, and no significant exploratory climate–groundwater relationship. The non-monotonic group patterns indicate that the available land-surface and climate indicators cannot independently explain the observed groundwater changes. The framework identifies priority areas for additional hydrogeological monitoring and management.

papers.title: Interplay of fabric anisotropy and drainage direction in soil–water retention behaviour of sand-silt mixtures
papers.summary: The soil–water retention curve (SWRC) is commonly treated as a material function in unsaturated soil analyses, although it may be affected by soil fabric and the drainage boundary condition imposed during laboratory testing. This study employs a coupled Discrete Element Method–Pore Network Model (DEM–PNM) framework to investigate the combined influence of fabric anisotropy and drainage direction on the water-retention behaviour of sand-silt mixtures. The model is first verified against experimental SWRCs reported for specimens subjected to different stress ratios. A systematic numerical program is then conducted on seven sand-silt mixtures with different grain-size distributions and three relative densities. Cylindrical specimens are prepared under different triaxial stress ratios to generate different stress-induced fabric states and pore-network anisotropy. Drying SWRCs are then simulated under three drainage configurations: one-dimensional bottom drainage, bottom-plus-lateral drainage, and full all-directional drainage. The results show that the pore-size distribution index, λ, remains largely insensitive to stress ratio and drainage condition. In contrast, the air-entry value (AEV) is affected by fabric anisotropy when drainage is restricted to a one-dimensional path, particularly when the major principal stress direction during specimen preparation is aligned with the drainage direction, a configuration commonly encountered in laboratory SWRC tests. For the lateral or full all-directional drainage configurations, numerical simulations indicate the effect of stress-induced anisotropy becomes negligible, as air invasion is governed by the most accessible boundary-connected pore pathways. Accordingly, a simple correction model is proposed to account for drainage-dependent AEV variation. Tracing soil–water signatures from contrasting land uses in low-flow streamwater of a mixed headwater catchment
papers.summary: Baseflow sustains water delivery from headwater catchments during non-event conditions and low flows. However, in mixed land-use headwater catchments, how land-use-related soil–water storage signatures are represented in low-flow streamwater and vary seasonally remain poorly understood. To address this gap, a two-year study involving monthly monitoring of a hilly purple-soil headwater catchment was conducted. We employed a combination of dissolved organic matter (DOM) fluorescence, stable water isotopes, and Bayesian mixing analysis to characterize source composition in low-flow streamwater, characterize temporal variation in dominant source signatures, and assess depth-related soil–water signatures under baseflow-dominated conditions. This study showed that orchard, sloping farmland, and paddy soil waters formed the main source-signature group, with a summed mean posterior attribution of 62.9% across the 19 retained samples, and summed monthly posterior-median attributions ranging from 52.7% to 72.8%, compared with a mean attribution of 10.7% to sampled valley shallow groundwater (monthly posterior-median range: 4.7%-26.1%). The dominant-source pattern showed seasonal variation among orchard, sloping farmland, and paddy soil waters, with estimated layer attributions favoring shallow layers (10 cm) in orchard and sloping farmland and middle layers (20–30 cm) in paddy; exploratory analyses indicated associations with bulk density and DOC. The findings indicate that different land-use types are associated with distinct soil–water storage signatures in low-flow streamwater, providing a basis for evaluating how future land-use changes may influence low-flow hydrological functioning.

papers.summary: The amount of impervious surfaces associated with urban development has increased, altering the natural flow of rainwater and reducing the amount of rainfall that can infiltrate into the ground. Concrete and bituminous roads also tend to direct much of the rainfall into the drainage system, thereby increasing surface runoff and reducing groundwater recharge. Pervious concrete pavement is an alternative approach where interconnected voids in the concrete allow water to flow through the pavement structure. This study investigates the possibility of pervious concrete pavement to improve infiltration and to contribute to the recharge of the phreatic zone. The main difference between pervious concrete and conventional concrete is the open-graded aggregate structure and limited or no use of fine aggregate. Thus, this network of interconnected pores provides a conduit for water movement through the pavement. Previous experimental studies have shown that the hydraulic performance of pervious concrete is greatly influenced by aggregate size, cement content, water-to-cement ratio, compaction, and void content. Field investigation of pervious concrete pavement in Ahmedabad indicated successful drainage and evaluated its strength, void ratio, permeability, and infiltration performance. The proposed method treats the pavement, granular sub-base, and underlying soil as an integrated infiltration system. Field studies of two-layer pervious concrete pavement systems have shown water infiltration through both the pervious concrete and the granular sub-base. Therefore, selecting the right pavement mix and sub-base is important to achieve sufficient permeability without sacrificing the required structural performance. The proposed system has the potential to reduce surface runoff, improve stormwater management, and provide an opportunity for groundwater recharge where site conditions permit.

papers.title: Benchmarking a new urban scheme in the ORCHIDEE 2.2 land surface model
papers.summary: Abstract. Urban areas change natural surface energy and water balances, yet some land surface models still represent cities as natural surfaces. In this study, we present the development of a one-tile urban scheme for the ORCHIDEE land surface model, designed to improve the representation of urban processes, particularly for high-resolution applications. The scheme incorporates key urban parameters such as albedo, building height, thermal properties, and imperviousness. We propose a novel physically-based approach for representing imperviousness, by modifying saturated hydraulic conductivity to account for both surface and subsurface impacts. Off-line simulations across 20 urban flux tower sites show improved performance in sensible and latent heat fluxes with the new urban scheme, compared to the original baresoil representation. Mean absolute error (MAE) evaluation confirms improved model skill, aligning with benchmark results from the Urban-PLUMBER intercomparison. The scheme also captures expected urban hydrological signatures, such as increased runoff, though some reductions in drainage may be less consistent with observed urban recharge patterns. This work lays the foundation for applying ORCHIDEE at the basin scale and in high-resolution convection-permitting for urban hydroclimate studies. Perspectives include refining thermal parameter choices, integrating anthropogenic heat fluxes, and conducting high-resolution simulations to assess hydrological performances using observed streamflow data.

papers.title: Runoff Discharge and Sedimentation Yield Assessment for Mine Drainage Design in Lateritic Nickel Mining
papers.source: RSF Conference Series Engineering and Technology
papers.summary: Laterite nickel mining using the open-pit method removes vegetation cover and exposes loose limonite materials, thereby increasing surface runoff and accelerating erosion and sedimentation. Without a quantitatively designed mine drainage system, these conditions may disrupt mining operations and reduce the quality of receiving water bodies. This study aimed to analyze runoff discharge, erosion rate, and sedimentation potential within a nickel mining area in Langgikima District, North Konawe Regency, Southeast Sulawesi, and to utilize the results as the basis for designing open channels and settling ponds. Twenty-one years of rainfall data (2005-2025) were analyzed to determine design rainfall and intensity using the Gumbel distribution and Mononobe equation. Runoff discharge, erosion, and sedimentation potential were estimated using the Rational Method, USLE, and SDR, respectively, and subsequently used to design mine drainage channels and settling ponds based on Manning's equation and Stokes' Law. The design rainfall was 187.26 mm with an intensity of 25.76 mm/h, classified as very heavy—six catchment areas ranging from 0.39 to 1.91 km² produced runoff discharges of 2.25 to 7.67 m³/s. Erosion rates were only 0.08 ton/ha/year in vegetated areas but increased to 66.47- 140.30 ton/ha/year in barren areas, with a total sedimentation potential of 4,012.7 m³/year. The combined channel carrying 13.288 m³/s requires a flow depth of 2.037 m and a bottom width of 2.353 m, whereas the settling pond requires an area of 1,247.7 m² and a storage volume of 6,238.3 m³, achieving a sediment removal efficiency of 91.23%.

papers.title: Rainfall-Driven Mobilization of Finite Sediment Storage and Two-Phase Debris-Flow Dynamics at Chalk Cliffs
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: This dataset contains the source code and processed model inputs supporting the study “Rainfall-Driven Mobilization of Finite Sediment Storage and Two-Phase Debris-Flow Dynamics at Chalk Cliffs.” The model links rainfall, infiltration, surface-water routing, sediment activation, and subsequent solid–liquid two-phase motion. Sediment activation depends on deposit instability and local surface-water availability. Activated sediment is progressively released from a finite prescribed inventory, with grains and pore water transferred to the moving phases under a saturated-release assumption. Subsequent motion accounts for terrain effects, interphase momentum exchange, liquid-phase Manning resistance, and solid-phase basal friction.The files include the C++ source code, model parameters, processed elevation and parameter rasters, rainfall forcing, and compilation and execution instructions. The supplied configuration represents the 4 July 2014 Chalk Cliffs event in Colorado, USA, using a 5 m grid and a simulation duration of 2000 s. This deposit contains simulation code and processed inputs; raw field observations and full simulation outputs are not included.

papers.title: A Three‐Dimensional Spatiotemporal Evolution Model for Two‐Phase Grouting Flow in Water‐Bearing Porous Media Based on the Forchheimer‐Modified Brinkman Equation
papers.source: International Journal for Numerical and Analytical Methods in Geomechanics
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Water‐bearing gravelly sand layers pose significant risks to underground construction due to their loose structure, high permeability, and susceptibility to seepage‐induced failure. To better understand and control grout migration in such formations, a three‐dimensional spatiotemporal model for grouting diffusion in water‐bearing porous media was developed using the Forchheimer‐modified Brinkman equation, with the level‐set method employed to capture the dynamic slurry‐water interface. The model incorporates viscous diffusion (Brinkman term) and inertial resistance (Forchheimer term), allowing characterization of both low‐Reynolds‐number shear‐dominated flow and nonlinear inertial effects at higher Reynolds numbers. The coupled framework simultaneously resolves the flow field, pressure field, and interface migration. Numerical simulations were compared with transparent‐chamber dynamic water grouting experiments and showed reasonable agreement in slurry diffusion morphology, pressure evolution, and asymmetric propagation in the with‐flow and against‐flow directions. Results show that the hydraulic gradient strongly controls slurry diffusion under flowing‐water conditions. The diffusion front advances farther downstream, while upstream propagation is restricted by hydraulic back pressure. The pressure field evolves from an initial transient state to a quasi‐steady regime, with pressure accumulation near the injection point and asymmetric attenuation along the flow direction. Slurry velocity decreases progressively with time, and high‐viscosity zones expand and shift downstream. The proposed model provides a useful numerical tool and theoretical basis for optimizing grouting design and predicting slurry diffusion in complex hydrogeological environments.

papers.title: A merging particle filter-based data assimilation for inverse estimation of soil hydraulic parameters from mini disk infiltrometer measurements
papers.summary: Soil hydraulic parameters, particularly the soil hydraulic conductivity and soil water characteristic curve (SWCC), play a critical role in hydrogeological investigations and rainfall-induced hazard assessment. However, conventional measurements are often time-consuming and difficult to implement under field conditions. This study proposes a practical data assimilation framework for rapid estimation of soil hydraulic parameters, which integrates mini disk infiltrometer (MDI) tests, three-dimensional finite element (FE) seepage simulations, and a merging particle filter (MPF) approach. A sequential updating strategy is further incorporated to assimilate information from multiple measurements and improve estimation robustness. The proposed framework is validated through laboratory soil column experiments involving Toyoura sand, silica sand K-5, and Masado soil. Time-series infiltration measurements obtained from MDI tests are assimilated into transient seepage simulations based on the Richards’ equation, and the estimated parameters are compared with independently measured SWCCs and hydraulic conductivities. The results demonstrate that the framework can accurately estimate soil hydraulic parameters using only MDI infiltration measurements, while Monte Carlo simulations (MCS) successfully reproduce measured infiltration responses with all NRMSE values below 20%. Furthermore, sensitivity analyses indicate that the estimation results are relatively insensitive to assimilation sequence, whereas assimilation quantity and prior uncertainty exert greater influence on parameter identifiability and convergence. Overall, the proposed framework provides a rapid and reliable approach for probabilistic characterization of soil hydraulic parameters and shows promising potential for large-scale hydrogeological investigations.

Relationship between land-use change and flow patterns: a duration curve analysis in the Babahoyo River basin, Ecuador
papers.source: Journal of South American Earth Sciences
papers.summary: Anthropogenic land use and land cover changes alter watershed hydrological processes by modifying the partitioning of precipitation into evapotranspiration, infiltration, and surface runoff. This study aimed to analyze the relationship between land-use change and flow regime in three sub-basins of the Babahoyo River basin, Ecuador, by using flow duration curves, Mann-Kendall test and Runoff coefficient: Zapotal (2,980 km 2 ), Echeandia (382 km 2 ), and San Pablo (1,387 km 2 ). Our investigation was based on a historical series of discharge data from 1998 to 2016, and its results showed expansion of short-cycle agriculture and reduction in natural forest cover. In the Zapotal and Echeandia sub-basins, natural forest gradually decreased from 2000 to 2016 and was replaced by agriculture; these two sub-basins are characterized by Andean soils. In the San Pablo River basin, there was also a 20% progressive increase (from 16% in 2000 to 36% in 2016) in natural forests, decreased by 78%. These changes were reflected in the flow duration curves and indicate increased hydrological variability, higher peak flows, and reduced baseflow, particularly in sub-basins with greater loss of vegetation cover. We concluded that the hydrological response to land use change varied among the basins: San Pablo showed more pronounced changes in its FDCs associated with substantial forest-cover reduction, whereas Echeandia exhibited comparatively moderate FDC changes despite losing approximately 90% of its natural forest cover, indicating that FDC changes do not necessarily scale proportionally with forest-cover loss. These results reinforce the importance of natural cover for the hydrological stability of sub-basins and highlight the need for differentiated conservation and management policies, adapted to the intensity and type of land-use changes in each basin.

Bok choy Brassica rapa L. subs. chinensis Brassicaceae, a widely cultivated vegetable in China, is commonly planted in the conventional greenhouses built with plastic films (PFs), IPNs and sliding doors (SDs), and named as PF-SD. However, the effectiveness of controlling agricultural insect pests in PF-SD greenhouse is low due to improper mesh sizes of IPNs and easily-deformative SDs. papers.title: Landfill Leachate Generation, Migration and Impacts on Soil and Groundwater Systems: A Review of Global, African and Nigerian Perspective
papers.source: IIARD INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF GEOGRAPHY AND ENVIRONMENTAL MANAGEMENT
papers.summary: Municipal solid waste generation is rising rapidly worldwide, and in many low- and middle income countries disposal remains dominated by open dumping without engineered containment, creating persistent conditions for the generation and uncontrolled migration of landfill leachate. This review synthesises global, African and Nigerian evidence on the composition, environmental behaviour and public health implications of landfill leachate, with particular attention to humid tropical and Niger Delta settings. Leachate composition is shown to evolve with waste age, climate and landfill design, shifting from organically dominated, high-BOD acidogenic-phase leachate towards ammonia- and chloride-dominated methanogenic-phase leachate over time. Once generated, contaminant transport is governed by the interaction of climate-driven infiltration, subsurface lithology and groundwater flow, conceptualised through the Source-Pathway-Receptor framework and explained mechanistically by Darcy's Law, Toth's groundwater flow system theory and the water balance concept. Within the Niger Delta and Port Harcourt specifically, high rainfall, unconsolidated sandy aquifers and shallow groundwater tables create conditions of especially high intrinsic vulnerability. papers.title: Geospatial Assessment of Land Use/Land Cover Dynamics in Wukari–Donga, Taraba State, Nigeria: Implications for Erosion Vulnerability
papers.summary: Land-use/land-cover (LULC) change is an important component of landscape transformation and may influence environmental conditions relevant to soil-erosion vulnerability. This study assessed the spatial and temporal dynamics of LULC in the Wukari–Donga area of Taraba State, Nigeria, for 2000, 2010 and 2024, and examined their potential implications for erosion vulnerability. Multi-temporal Landsat imagery, supported by Sentinel-2 imagery for training-sample identification and verification, was processed in ArcGIS Pro. Seven LULC classes—water, trees/savanna woodland, flooded vegetation, cropland, built-up area, bare ground and rangeland—were mapped using supervised Maximum Likelihood Classification. Area statistics, percentage changes and cross-tabulation were used to assess the spatial extent and temporal dynamics of the classes. In 2024, rangeland was the dominant class, covering 4,249.71 km² (60.94%), followed by cropland (1,285.25 km²; 18.43%) and trees/savanna woodland (1,240.68 km²; 17.79%). Between 2000 and 2024, tree/savanna woodland declined by 52.76% and cropland by 30.66%, whereas rangeland increased by 75.08%. Built-up area, bare ground, flooded vegetation and water bodies increased by 2,077.56%, 3,595.26%, 587.17% and 31.85%, respectively, although the large relative increases in built-up area and bare ground reflected their very small initial extents. LULC change was not uniform: cropland and tree cover increased between 2000 and 2010 but declined substantially during 2010–2024, while rangeland followed the opposite trajectory. The results demonstrate substantial landscape reorganization and identify changes in vegetation, cultivated and exposed surfaces that may influence erosion vulnerability. The findings provide a geospatial basis for sustainable land-use planning and soil-resource management in the Wukari–Donga area.

papers.title: Experimental evaluation of wicking geotextile and grass for moisture control in subgrade with silty clay
papers.summary: After years of operation, subgrade generally equilibrates to a moisture content that is higher than the optimum value. This study explored the influence of geotextile and grass on the moisture reduction and mechanical properties of silty clay. The experimental results showed that installing wicking geotextile effectively reduced the volumetric water content (VWC) by 2% at the monitored depths. By applying another wicking geotextile, the VWC at a depth of 170 mm was reduced further. The combination of grass and geotextile notably optimized the moisture migration, particularly in reducing the VWC around the wicking geotextile. Compared with the control case, the residual matric suction at a depth of 170 mm increased by 12.6, 16.9, and 23.7 kPa in the single-geotextile, double-geotextile, and geotextile–grass cases, respectively. In addition, the single-geotextile case exhibited an average increase of 6.4% in the shear wave velocity (SWV), whereas the geotextile–grass case demonstrated an increase of 9.8%. The higher SWV indicates that the geotextile–grass system helped to mitigate the loss of small-strain stiffness of the silty clay after rainfall infiltration. Furthermore, the high suction at the root–geotextile interface indicates that the geotextile–grass system is an effective approach for improving moisture drainage.

papers.title: Soil and Water Conservation Mechanism in Oil Palm Plantations: A Review of Best Management Practices and Decision Support Strategies
papers.source: WSEAS TRANSACTIONS ON ENVIRONMENT AND DEVELOPMENT
papers.summary: Soil and water conservation on oil palm plantation is increasingly considered as a glimmer of hope for the future sustainability of land functionality and environment. Appropriate management practices and informed decision-making frameworks thus have a strong influence on conservation outcomes. This study aims to systematically identify, categorize, synthesize and quantitatively aggregate peer-reviewed evidence regarding soil and water conservation mechanisms in oil palm plantations, focusing on best management practice strategies and decision support. This study uses Systematic Litigation Review (SLR) the Scopus database is used as a reference in searching scientific publication. A keyword-based structured search was used to identify peer-reviewed articles published from 2020 to 2025 and subsequent screening in sequence based on relevance and language. Thirty-eight articles met all the selection criteria for analysis. Then we extracted data and analyzed it using thematic synthesis with descriptive quantitative aggregation of reported metrics (soil loss, SOC change, runoff reduction, or yield response). The results show six main interrelated themes: control of soil erosion; soil fertility and organic matter management; conservation of water and hydrological regulation; integrated land use and landscape management; agronomic best methods practices; and support for decision-making processes. Quantitative synthesis show that cover-based and structural BMPs decrease soil loss by 50–80%, organic amendments increase SOC by 10–35% and integrated water management decreases runoff by 20–60% across regions reported.

Engineering of Problematic Soils
papers.summary: Soil behaviour is governed by composition, structure, fabric and pore fluid properties, and it evolves under changing loads and environmental conditions. Yet, as the book emphasises, “problematic soils do not conform to the ideal soil used in classical soil mechanics theories,” requiring approaches that extend far beyond standard design codes. Engineering of Problematic Soils: Problematic Engineering Soils explains how soils form, are transported and deposited, and how geological, climatic and anthropogenic processes shape their engineering behaviour. It examines organic, expansive, collapsible, residual, glacial and anthropogenic soils showing why their heterogeneity, metastability and sensitivity challenge investigation, sampling and modelling. Environmental and human induced changes, from climate driven extremes to construction activity and groundwater changes, are shown to alter stresses and saturation, often triggering geotechnical hazards. A strategic framework sets out multi stage investigation, robust ground modelling and risk based, numerically informed design to create safe, resilient and sustainable geotechnical infrastructure.

papers.title: Canopy water delivery and soil physical–hydrological functioning across forest restoration and Eucalyptus stand-development stages in a Cerrado–Atlantic Forest transition
papers.summary: Understanding how vegetation cover, stand development, and prior land-use history are associated with soil physical–hydrological functioning is essential for interpreting runoff regulation in human-modified tropical landscapes. We evaluated rainfall delivery to the soil surface, soil physical condition, infiltration, and surface runoff across five vegetation conditions in a Cerrado–Atlantic Forest transition in southeastern Brazil: a native forest remnant, two enriched restoration stands, and two Eucalyptus plantations representing contrasting stages of stand development and land-use trajectories. Open rainfall and throughfall were monitored over an annual cycle, while soil water content, bulk density, total porosity, soil penetration resistance, infiltration rate, and surface runoff were repeatedly measured in replicated plots. These indicators were further integrated into a standardized Soil Physical Infiltration Potential Index (SPI) to summarize infiltration-favorable versus restrictive soil states. Throughfall increased linearly with rainfall in all vegetation conditions, but cumulative throughfall-to-rainfall ratios differed among covers, indicating contrasting canopy water-delivery patterns. Soil physical indicators showed clearer separation among vegetation conditions than surface runoff alone. The native forest remnant exhibited the most favorable soil conditions, with higher soil water content and total porosity and lower bulk density and penetration resistance, and also showed the highest SPI. In contrast, the younger Eucalyptus stand exhibited the most restrictive conditions and the lowest SPI, while the restoration stands and the 39-month Eucalyptus stand occupied intermediate positions. Variation of soil physical properties under tea gardens along an alluvial toposequence in Northern Vietnam
papers.summary: Soil structural and hydraulic properties are fundamental for regulating water retention, aeration, saturated hydraulic conductivity (Ks), and root development in perennial cropping systems. This study evaluated the spatial variability of soil physical properties in tea plantation systems developed along contrasting alluvial geomorphic settings in northern Vietnam. The study was conducted along a representative alluvial toposequence in Tan Cuong commune, Thai Nguyen province, including riverside lowlands, previous dikes, and older hillslope positions. papers.title: Impact of Soil Data Representation on Streamflow Modelling: A Contiguous-Object Connectivity Approach Case Study in Switzerland
papers.summary: Hydrological models often rely on soil data to represent water partitioning, storage and release within a catchment. However, differences in soil data representation may be obscured by calibration when performance is evaluated primarily against streamflow. This study investigates how alternative soil datasets influence streamflow performance, internal hydrological processes, and parameter sensitivity in a Contiguous-Object Connectivity Approach (COCOA) Soil and Water Assessment Tool Plus (SWAT+) model of an agricultural catchment in Switzerland. Three otherwise identical model setups use a) a global low-resolution soil dataset (World-Soil), b) a national medium-resolution dataset (Swiss-Soil), and c) a high-resolution local soil dataset (Local-Soil). COCOA maintains identical spatial modelling units across scenarios, separating soil-data effects from changes in model discretisation. Before calibration, the three soil scenarios produce pronounced differences in water partitioning: World-Soil produces the greatest surface runoff, Swiss-Soil the greatest subsurface-flow contributions, and Local-Soil the highest evapotranspiration. After calibration, streamflow performance converges, with comparable relative Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency values across scenarios and higher Kling–Gupta efficiency for Swiss-Soil. Nevertheless, contrasting water balance partitioning, soil-water storage, and groundwater-release behaviour persist. Soil-data effects are also more apparent under median- and low-flow conditions than during high flows. These results show that similar outlet-streamflow performance can mask substantial differences in simulated catchment functioning. Soil datasets should therefore be selected according to the intended modelling objective, and internal hydrological diagnostics should complement conventional streamflow-performance metrics.

papers.title: Heterogeneous soils – residual soils
papers.summary: Residual soils formed by physical and chemical weathering processes in situ are heterogeneous soils which vary spatially in properties and composition and vary from completely weathered rock to highly weathered rock. Extensive deposits are found in the tropics but these soils occur in all climatic zones. They can be difficult to sample and test, are partially saturated, have weak bonds, are highly permeable, and exhibit swelling, collapse and loss of strength when subject to changes in effective stress or water content. Properties of residual soils are affected by the test preparation process. Therefore, correlations developed for sedimentary soils may not apply to residual soils. Current properties are not related to stress history since the solids volume decreases as a result of weathering. They can show similar characteristics to overconsolidated soils when loaded but this is due to particle bonding, a result of partial saturation or chemical bonding. They can be in a metastable state which will collapse when sheared, stable-contractive state which causes small strains until yield point when significant straining occurs, or in stable-dilatant state when soil expands when sheared. Residual soil can exhibit fine-grained and coarse-grained behaviour. Collapse of partially saturated residual soils is prevented by controlling infiltration and groundwater. Rainfall induced slope failures are common in residual soils.

papers.title: Management of headwater catchments: cultural background, science and policy
papers.summary: Headwater catchments serve as water towers and initial regulatory buffers against hydrometeorological hazards, yet they face several forms of degradation from unsustainable land use and accelerating climate change. We argue that effective headwater control requires an integrated approach combining watershed governance, science, policy, and cultural background. Old societies showed considerable capacity to solve hydraulic problems but did not fully understand watershed runoff formation and downstream impacts. Effective ecological engineering in headwaters still requires a better understanding of detailed processes in the soil-vegetation complex and wider land use concerns. Religion and environmental ethics intersect as global faith traditions support ecological conservation as a moral imperative influencing how communities perceive, value, and protect natural resources. However, cultural and ethical values alone may be constrained by short-term human interests, human-centered worldviews, and social instability. Their contribution to headwater protection therefore depends on how such values are translated into community participation, land-use decisions, and locally adapted governance. Compared to blanket legislative regulation of ‘Protected Headwater Areas’, our case studies suggest a more effective strategy concentrated on a particular catchment outlet and combining technical, ecological and governance measures. Progress in the management of headwater catchments is contingent upon the involvement of local communities through a participatory process with locally adapted governance, interdisciplinary understanding, and a focus on ecosystem services. Thus, sustainable headwater management requires not only scientific knowledge and regulatory instruments, but also their integration with local participation and culturally embedded environmental values.

papers.summary: Physics-based simulation underpins engineering analysis but remains difficult to deploy in practice due to complex setup, parameterization, and interpretation. The novelty of this study lies in the quantitative evaluation of an existing pump-fed canal under increased discharge conditions by linking field-measured hydraulic conditions, sedimentation and roughness, and rehabilitation scenarios using SOBEK-1D. papers.summary: Abstract Estimating groundwater age is vital for water management, especially in semi-arid regions, where aquifers are the primary freshwater source. Radiocarbon ( 14 C) dating of dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) is widely used to estimate groundwater age, assuming DIC is derived mainly from modern soil CO 2 , while soil carbonate contributions are considered 14 C-dead. However, in semi-arid regions, soil carbonates contributing to DIC in unsaturated zone soil water (UZSW) may contain measurable 14 C activity. This can impart an apparent age which is different from that assumed in conventional correction models and thus needs to be properly accounted for in groundwater age estimations. Here, we measured 14 C and δ 13 C in DIC in UZSW, soil CO 2 , soil carbonates, and soil organic matter to identify DIC sources and assess their impact on groundwater dating. Results show that the ages of DIC in UZSW range from 90 to 2290 years, with an average of ∼1240 years in semi-arid western India. We estimated that ∼13% of DIC derives from soil carbonates with 14 C ages in the range of 3500–14,000 BP in this region. These findings suggest that 14 C-based groundwater age estimates, particularly for groundwater younger than 10,000 years, may be biased if the 14 C activity of soil carbonates are not adequately accounted for. Our study also highlights the analytical challenges associated with isolating DIC for 14 C measurements. Overall, our results underscore the importance of characterizing the 14 C signature of soil carbonates and incorporating it into groundwater dating frameworks to improve the reliability of groundwater age determinations.

papers.title: Nonlocal interactions through hydrodynamics drive biofilm development and microbial competition in porous media
papers.summary: Abstract Microorganisms predominantly exist within soil-like environments as sessile communities called biofilms, where fluid dynamics critically shape their development and dispersal. Despite their central role in diverse systems, from biogeochemical processes to industrial filtration, oil recovery, groundwater contamination, and carbon sequestration, the mechanisms underlying biofilm-flow interactions in porous media remain poorly understood. Here, we combine microfluidic experiments with mathematical modeling to demonstrate that nonlocal interactions through hydrodynamic effects mediate intricate spatiotemporal dynamics and drive exploitative competition within porous media. Our results show that biofilms self-organize into clusters of biologically clogged channels interspersed with preferential flow paths (PFPs). PFP formation and stability result from feedbacks between local changes in hydraulic conductivity and global reorganization of flow patterns and pressure distribution. We reveal that PFPs tend to be unstable, with detachment of biofilm triggered when pressure differentials exceed critical thresholds. Based on simulations of competing populations, we suggest that these large-scale detachment events could be interpreted as an evolutionary trade-off, whereby bacterial matrices are sufficiently robust to withstand continuous shear stress while remaining sensitive to pressure-induced failure, thereby enabling nutrient access and avoiding redirection of resources toward competitors. The nonlocal nature of these hydrodynamic interactions shows that fitness in porous media must be thought of as a multiscale concept and provides new insights into bacterial adaptation strategies in porous environments. These findings further suggest targeted approaches for biofilm control in both natural and engineered systems.

papers.summary: ABSTRACT The Barcelona Basic Model (BBM) is the most well‐known elasto‐plastic constitutive model for describing the behavior of unsaturated soils. However, the selection of BBM parameters from laboratory data remains challenging due to the strong coupling and interdependence among the constitutive parameters governing hydro‐mechanical behavior. In this context, the Design of Experiments (DOE) methodologies provide a systematic approach for quantifying parameter influence and reducing the dimensionality of calibration problems. This paper presents a sensitivity analysis of the parameters used in the coupled hydro‐mechanical numerical simulation of a suction‐controlled oedometer test for three distinct soils, enabled by a computational framework designed to automatically execute and manage many simulations. The analyses were performed using both exhaustive Full Factorial (FF) designs and reduced Plackett–Burman (PB) matrices. The investigated variables included BBM mechanical parameters and hydraulic parameters, while the response variable was the simulated vertical strain during oedometric loading. The FF analyses were used as reference and PB matrices with different numbers of trials were subsequently assessed regarding their ability to reproduce the patterns obtained from the FF analyses with fewer simulations. The results showed that the soil stiffness parameters λ(0) and r , together with the historical variable p 0 * , had the greatest influence on vertical strain across all three soils. In contrast, hydraulic parameters had little to no effect on the response variable in this case. The results demonstrate that DOE methodologies provide an effective and computationally efficient framework for sensitivity assessment and parameter prioritization in coupled hydro‐mechanical simulations involving unsaturated soils.

papers.title: Macroscopic and mesoscopic mechanical behavior of the interface between piles and unsaturated sand under vertical cyclic loading
papers.summary: Understanding the degradation of pile bearing capacity under vertical cyclic loading requires an in-depth investigation of the pile–unsaturated sand interface. This study employs a multi-scale approach—combining visualized cyclic loading tests, particle image velocimetry (PIV), and discrete element method (DEM) simulations—to elucidate the underlying macro–meso evolutionary mechanisms. Laboratory results identify an optimal water content of 8%, which maximizes interfacial effective stress and bearing capacity, while cumulative settlement is shown to stabilize beyond a critical threshold of 400 cycles. A key transitional mechanism is observed at a depth of 180 mm, where an initial spike in excess pore water pressure triggers transient strength degradation, followed by localized particle densification that restores stability. Kinematic analysis via PIV confirms that soil deformation propagates radially from the pile tip, mitigated significantly by matric suction. Crucially, DEM simulations correlate these macroscopic behaviors to mesoscopic load-transfer mechanisms, revealing the formation of a structural compaction core zone at the pile tip sustained by dense force chains. By clarifying the synergistic process of initial cyclic weakening and subsequent stabilization, this study provides a robust theoretical framework for the long-term performance assessment and design optimization of pile foundations.

papers.title: Hydrogeochemical, Microbial, and Rainfall Datasets for Anaerobic Dechlorination in Salinity-Gradient Aquifers
papers.summary: Climate change–driven sea-level rise and extreme rainfall events increase the risk of groundwater salinization of aquifers, posing challenges to in situ anaerobic bioremediation of chlorinated solvents. This dataset documents anaerobic reductive dechlorination across salinity gradients (electrical conductivity: 118–10,300 μS/cm) at three chlorinated solvent-contaminated sites in Taiwan, monitored from March to August 2019. The three sites represent contrasting salinity conditions and remediation strategies, including biostimulation and monitored natural attenuation. Measurements include multilevel hydraulic conductivity, time-series hydrogeochemical variables, volatile organic compounds, and microbial community data, including 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, quantitative analysis of Dehalococcoides and functional genes ( tceA , vcrA , bvcA , hupL ), and total bacterial counts, with propidium monoazide pretreatment applied to distinguish viable populations. Daily rainfall and temperature records from nearby meteorological stations are also provided. This six-month dataset provides a field baseline for assessing salinity effects on dechlorinating communities and for developing models linking hydrogeochemistry, seasonal hydrological variation, and microbial processes in salinity-impacted aquifers.

Closed-Form Solutions for Temperature-Dependent Suction Stress under Transient Infiltration in Unsaturated Soil: An Application for Stability Analysis of Strip Plate Anchors
papers.summary: Abstract The soil layer up to a certain depth below the ground surface exists in an unsaturated state, where factors such as precipitation, evaporation, and prolonged subsurface heat waves control the state and material properties of soil. The suction stress that contributes to the resistance of the soil mass governs the stability of geostructures and depends on the thermal and hydraulic interactions in unsaturated soil. No solutions are available to determine the suction stress in soils subjected to transient flow conditions at elevated temperatures. This study develops closed-form expressions for temperature-dependent suction stress under transient flow conditions using the one-dimensional transient flow equation and a temperature-dependent soil–water retention curve. The developed equation was implemented within the framework of stress-based finite-element limit analysis to evaluate the stability of strip plate anchors in terms of their uplift capacity embedded in unsaturated sand, silt, and clay under transient flow conditions and varying temperatures. The critical role of thermal and hydraulic interactions in different types of unsaturated soils (clay, silt, and sand), specifically regarding matric suction, effective degree of saturation, and suction stress over time, has been discussed in detail. Additionally, a comprehensive parametric study has been conducted to evaluate the effects of transient flow and elevated temperature on the uplift capacity of shallow strip plate anchors. The results indicate that the behavior of plate anchors in unsaturated sand and silt is distinctly different from that in clay.

FLOWS: a model to simulate water and solutes fluxes in agricultural and environmental systems: 2. Modules for specific applications in water and nutrient management
papers.summary: Abstract This paper is the second of two companion studies. The first paper focused on describing the model FLOWS, theory and the model benchmarking. This paper addresses FLOWS modules on specific applications: irrigation, temperature, organic carbon processes and nutrient transformation and transport in the soil. It also includes applications of FLOWS model in real scenarios. In the irrigation module, FLOWS allows for different scenarios: (1) no irrigation, i.e., only rainfall; (2) irrigation introduced by the user as a top-boundary, temporally variable, input flux; (3) irrigation computed as the daily potential evapotranspiration demand; and (4) irrigation computed by the model. In the latter, FLOWS optimizes irrigation fluxes and schedule according to a criterion based on the average pressure head along a user-specified depth, e.g., the root zone. Since soil temperature influences several soil processes, FLOWS simulates the temperature distribution in depth and time by using a solution to heat flow equations proposed by van Wijk and De Vries. FLOWS simulates fertilizer applications as organic matter (manure and crop residues) or mineral fertilizers. It can either simulate organic matter decomposition with coupled carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus transformations governed by C:N and C:P ratios or simulate nitrogen transport alone using an empirical mineralization approach independent on organic matter dynamics. Two applications of the model are presented in this paper: (1) analysing the role of spatial variability in soil and vegetation for large-scale irrigation optimization, and (2) monitoring and modelling water and nutrient fluxes from irrigated fields to the surface drainage network. In the first application, FLOWS proved reliable for optimizing irrigation at large scales by accounting for the spatial variability of soil and vegetation properties and by enabling the analysis of the uncertainty associated with progressively overlooking this variability. papers.title: Influence of Fines Plasticity and Water Content on the Mechanical Response of Binary Soil Mixtures: Analysis Using the Equivalent Void Ratio
papers.source: Journal of Geotechnical and Geoenvironmental Engineering
papers.summary: Abstract The mechanical behavior of sand–fines mixtures, particularly under various fines plasticity and water content, is not yet fully understood. This study experimentally investigated the mechanical behavior of sand–fines mixtures with various fines content (FC), water content, and fines plasticity, reflecting the unsaturated and heterogeneous nature of natural soils. Bender element tests, in conjunction with one-dimensional compression tests, were conducted on mixtures of silica sand with three distinct fines types: nonplastic silica flour, plastic kaolin clay, and plastic Korean red clay. These mixtures were prepared across a range of water contents (0%–10%) and FC of up to 30%. The results reveal that with increasing FC, mixtures containing nonplastic fines consistently exhibited a reduction in stiffness, regardless of the water content. In contrast, those with plastic fines exhibited an increase in the shear wave velocity under low-water-content conditions, a phenomenon attributed to suction-induced interparticle bonding. The contribution of fines to the load-carrying soil skeleton was examined using the equivalent void ratio concept. Through back-analysis, the fitted b parameter, which represents the structural role of fines, demonstrated a strong, nonlinear percolation-type correlation with matric suction. This finding suggests that in partially saturated conditions, the b parameter, when considered in conjunction with matric suction, provides a physically meaningful and practical indicator for assessing the structural contribution of fines in unsaturated granular mixtures. This study advances the understanding of complex soil behavior and has significant implications for the characterization of natural soils.
