papers.summary: Capillary-driven transport in porous media plays a fundamental role in a wide range of natural and engineered systems, including heat pipes, fibrous and ceramic materials, soils, contaminant transport in the vadose zone, and moisture-management technologies. Although substantial progress has been made in modeling and characterizing wicking under simplified conditions, important gaps remain in understanding how thermal gradients, partial saturation, and evaporation-driven solute cycling influence liquid transport in porous media. This dissertation addresses these gaps through a combined experimental, analytical, and numerical investigation of capillary-driven flow in porous materials across thermal, engineered, and environmental settings.The first part of this dissertation develops a Richards equation-based numerical framework to model moisture infusion in porous ceramics and other engineered materials by incorporating capillary pressure–saturation and relative permeability relationships. The model was validated against high-resolution neutron microscope imaging experiments and two independent analytical solutions. Extended simulations were then performed to investigate the role of engineered wettability — including hydrophilic surface coatings and hydrophobic inclusions — on two-dimensional moisture migration patterns. These results demonstrate how material design and local wettability modification can be used to control liquid transport pathways in porous systems. The second part of this work investigates non-isothermal wicking in porous media. Experiments were conducted using sintered polymer-bead wicks and hydrocarbon liquids under imposed temperature differences between the liquid and the wick. A sharp-front Darcy-based framework was developed to model the transient rise of liquid while accounting for temperature-dependent viscosity, surface tension, and density. papers.title: Impacts of Cover Crops, No-Tillage and Cotton-Sorghum Rotation on Soil-Water Dynamics: Environmental and Economic Implications
papers.summary: Water scarcity associated with declining groundwater levels in the Ogallala Aquifer threatens the long-term sustainability of irrigated agriculture in the semi-arid Texas High Plains. As irrigation capacity decreases, management strategies that improve soil-mediated water capture and enhance production resilience are increasingly important. This thesis integrates a regional literature synthesis with field-based evaluation of conservation practices aimed at improving water-use efficiency in cotton-based cropping systems. The literature identifies irrigation technology improvements, precision agriculture technologies, and soil health management as key pathways for reducing water demand and enhancing precipitation capture, while also emphasizing economic constraints and site-specific performance of conservation practices. A two-year field study assessed the short-term effects of cover crops and cotton–sorghum rotation under no-tillage on soil physical properties, crop productivity, and economic indicators. Soil measurements included saturated hydraulic conductivity, aggregate stability, compaction, and total organic carbon, alongside cotton and sorghum yield and fiber quality. Results showed limited short-term changes in most soil properties, although aggregate stability increased under rotational systems with cover crops. Cotton yield remained consistent across treatments, but fiber quality and associated economic returns declined in rotation-based systems. Sorghum performance was largely influenced by interannual climatic variability rather than management effects. Overall, findings suggest that while conservation practices hold potential to improve soil function and water-use efficiency, measurable agronomic and economic benefits may require long-term adoption. Extended evaluation is necessary to determine whether gradual soil health improvements can enhance system resilience and profitability under increasing water limitations.

papers.title: Hydraulic anisotropy of unsaturated soil
papers.summary: Hydraulic anisotropy in unsaturated soils significantly influences rainfall-induced slope failures, yet limited research has characterized its variation with depth. This study examines the hydraulic anisotropy of a layered unsaturated soil profile from 0.5m to 3.0m depth at 0.5m intervals and quantifies its impact on slope stability under transient infiltration. Laboratory characterization included index properties, Soil-Water Characteristic Curve (SWCC) and saturated permeability measurements for both vertical and horizontal flow directions. Results revealed consistent hydraulic anisotropy (Kr = Kₕ/Kv) ranging from 1.15 to 1.91 across depths, with highest anisotropy near the surface decreasing with depth due to overburden compression. Fines content exhibited a strong inverse relationship with permeability, reaching a minimum of 1.61×10−8 m/s at 1.5m depth where fines peaked at 59%. Numerical modeling using GeoStudio (SEEP/W and SLOPE/W) simulated 12-day rainfall (20 mm/day) followed by 12-day evaporation for 30° and 45° slopes under isotropic and anisotropic conditions. Results demonstrate that anisotropic conditions consistently produced lower factors of safety than isotropic assumptions at the critical Day 12 minimum, with the most pronounced effect observed on the 30° slope with a shallow slip surface, where anisotropy reduced the FoS by approximately 27.3%. For 45° slopes, reductions of 6.6% and 7.3% were recorded for deep-seated and shallow surfaces respectively, while the 30° deep- seated case showed a negligible difference of less than 1.0%. This research highlights that incorporating depth-dependent anisotropic hydraulic properties is essential for accurate rainfall- induced slope failure assessment.

papers.title: Modified Geogrid for Geobarrier System Incorporating Unsaturated Soil
papers.summary: The Geobarrier System (GBS) is a three-component system to improve slope stability by combining capillary barrier, retaining system and vegetative cover. Currently, the retaining system of the conventional configuration is mainly controlled by the geogrid. However, the embedment length of the geogrid requires massive excavation which also leads to the longer construction duration. Considering this limitation, reducing the length of the geogrid while maintaining sufficient stability became the primary objective of this study. On the other hand, although earth nailing systems have been widely applied in slope stabilization practice, integration between geogrid reinforcement and earth mechanical anchorage has not been demonstrated within a unified framework. Therefore, J-pin attachments to the tip of geogrid are introduced in this study to compensate for the tensile resistance loss of the reduced geogrid embedment length. To conduct this, the conventional model with geogrid embedment length of 0.7 times the slope’s height (H) was modified into 0.6 H, 0.5 H, and 0.4 H. Attachment of J-pins were carried out gradually from the lowest layer of the geogrid. Analysis was conducted with two finite element software: PLAXIS 2D and ABAQUS, each with different purposes. PLAXIS 2D was utilized to perform unsaturated seepage analysis and mechanical analysis for calibration of ABAQUS numerical control settings. ABAQUS was used to perform mechanical analysis calibrated from PLAXIS 2D for modified models with J-pin attachments. Results show that modification on the geogrid embedment length has no significant influence on the pore-water pressure. papers.title: Finite Element Method Simulations of Redox Processes in Nanoporous Gold and in Lithium Batteries
papers.source: Carl von Ossiezky University of Oldenburg
papers.summary: This thesis investigates the transport phenomena in nanoporous electrodes and in lithium electrodes using a combination of scanning electrochemical microscopy (SECM) and finite element method (FEM) simulations. The primary goal is to develop and validate analytical models that accurately describe key properties such as porosity, film thickness, and current density distribution in electrochemical systems with complex geometries. Initial studies are devoted to heterogeneous models of nanoporous gold (NPG) and platinum on carbon (Pt/C), highlighting how variations in pore structure impact electrochemical responses. These findings led to the development of improved analytical equations that capture the dynamics of mass transport more effectively. Subsequently, homogeneous models are introduced to simplify the representation of transport by diffusion properties while maintaining accuracy across a range of porosities. A new analytical equation for SECM approach curves was developed, validated through simulations, and shown to be applicable under diverse experimental conditions. The thesis further examines lithium electrodes and SEI evolution using numerical simulations to model the secondary current density distribution under realistic conditions. The results demonstrate how probe positioning and geometry affect the local current density distribution and data interpretation, offering practical guidance for minimizing measurement artefacts in SEI studies. Overall, this work provides valuable tools for optimizing electrode design and contributes to advancing high-performance electrochemical systems.

papers.title: Assessing the influence of rainfall-induced desiccation cracking on slope stability in Malaysia
papers.summary: The influence of climate change on slope stability has become increasingly relevant in recent years, particularly in tropical regions like Malaysia, where the frequency and severity of rainfall events are anticipated to vary considerably. This study examined the combined impacts of rainfall variability and soil desiccation cracking on the slope stability in Malaysia’s tropical granitic residual soils. The study conducted a comprehensive analysis of precipitation patterns utilizing both historical and projected climatic data across multiple climate change scenarios. It subsequently investigated the formation of desiccation cracks in soils exposed to repeated cycles of wetting and drying under controlled laboratory circumstances, replicating actual seasonal variations. Numerical models evaluated the impact of rainfall infiltration on slope stability amid changing climatic circumstances. The rainfall pattern analysis revealed a notable tendency of increasing wet-season rainfall but a considerable decline in dry-season precipitation. This extreme climate condition has provoked the formation of desiccation cracks on soil slopes. The subsequent experimental study indicated that desiccation cracks substantially enhance water infiltration into the soil. The mechanism involved increased crack formation with the repetitive wetting-drying cycles, leading to increased void ratio in soil, and hence resulted in a higher permeability. The numerical analysis reported that slopes with gentler gradients exhibited less sensitivity to climate change impact, with average Factor of Safety (FOS) values of about 0.8, 0.95, and 1.1 for slopes of 1V:1H, 1V:1.5H, and 1V:2H, respectively, under future rainfall conditions. papers.source: University of Southern Queensland ePrints (University of Southern Queensland)
papers.summary: Permanent raised bed (PRB) farming systems combine several elements (e.g. reduced tillage, controlled traffic, stubble retention) of conservation agriculture. PRB systems have recently been introduced into irrigated areas but there is a lack of information on the agronomic and irrigation performance of these systems under these conditions. Three years of field research into the performance of irrigated PRBs was conducted in south east Queensland, Australia and north west Pakistan. These studies benchmarked the irrigation performance of variously sized PRB systems and explored the impact of bed renovation method (no tillage (NT), shallow cultivation (SC) and blade ploughing (BP)) on soil hydro-physical properties (bulk density, soil moisture storage, infiltration), irrigation performance, crop yield and input water productivity (WP). Irrigation management strategies to improve lateral infiltration and irrigation performance were also investigated. The initial benchmarking study was conducted on two farms with clayey Vertisol (Australia) and three farms with sandy clay loam, Alfisol, (Pakistan) soils. The results showed low irrigation performance with excessive deep drainage potential. The irrigation application efficiency (Ea) on the clayey Vertisol and sandy clay loam was as low as 68% and 50%, requirement efficiency (Er) 96% and 77% and distribution uniformity (DU) 86% and 66%, respectively. However, the majority of the narrow beds (66 cm furrow spacing) were over-irrigated on the sandy clay loam while the wide beds (132 cm furrow spacing) were under-irrigated. Inappropriate renovation and bed furrow dimensions, sub-optimal irrigation management and poor lateral infiltration were the main factors likely to affect WP of irrigated PRBs. papers.summary: ABSTRACT Soil erosion is a major cause of land degradation in Ethiopia, leading to declining soil fertility and agricultural productivity. To address this problem, the government has promoted the large-scale implementation of physical soil and water conservation structures. This study evaluated the effectiveness of these conservation measures in Silti District by examining their technical suitability and their influence on selected soil physicochemical properties across different slope positions. Field surveys and laboratory analyses were conducted. A topographic transect walk was used to assess conservation structures across upper, middle, and lower slope categories. Structural parameters such as bund height, top width, and spacing were measured, and soil samples were collected for analysis of bulk density, soil organic carbon, soil reaction, and selected soil nutrients. The results showed clear variation in soil conditions along the slope gradient. Soils on gentle slopes where conservation measures were relatively well maintained had lower bulk density (1.19 g/cm³), higher soil organic carbon (2.88%), and relatively better nutrient availability. In contrast, soils on steep slopes exhibited higher bulk density (up to 1.65 g/cm³), lower organic carbon content, reduced nutrient levels, and more acidic conditions, indicating soil degradation. Comparison of soil bund dimensions with national Ministry of Agriculture standards revealed that although some parameters met the recommended specifications, deviations were observed in top width and spacing, which may reduce structural effectiveness. These inconsistencies are likely associated with limited technical knowledge during construction. The study highlights the need to prioritize the technical quality and proper design of conservation structures through improved technical support, monitoring, and farmer training to ensure long-term sustainability of soil and water conservation efforts.

This doctoral research focused on integrated frameworks to improve irrigation scheme performance and sustainability by combining hydraulic performance improvement options, soil salinity identification and spatial mapping, and developing models of crop yield and economic gains depending on the agricultural water, soil, and nutrients. papers.summary: Slope failures, particularly failures shallow in depth, that occur following intense rainfall and infiltration are closely related to unsaturated conditions. In January and February of 2023, Auckland experienced numerous rainfall-induced slope failures following two extraordinary rainfall events: the Auckland Anniversary Floods and Cyclone Gabrielle. One area subject to numerous small- and large-scale rainfall-induced slope failures was the Awhitu Peninsula, which is predominantly underlain by Awhitu Sands. A slope failure that occurred along Awhitu Road was selected as the study area for this research. papers.title: Food Insecurity and the Role of Drought and Soil Erosion: a Case Study, North West Ethiopia
papers.summary: Food insecurity remains a persistent challenge in rural Ethiopia, particularly in rain-fed agricultural areas such as the Libokemkem and Ebinat districts in Northwestern Ethiopia. Despite decades of development interventions, many households continue to face limited access to sufficient and nutritious food, low dietary diversity, and constrained livelihood opportunities. Interconnected factors, including socioeconomic marginalization, climate variability, and environmental degradation, drive these challenges. To better understand these complex relationships, this thesis adopts an integrated approach that links household food security with climatic and environmental conditions.
